Physical Quantities

Joseph Fourier (21 March 1768 – 30 May 1830) was
a French mathematician and physicist. Fourier was
born at Auxerre as a son of a tailor. He lost both his
parents at the age of 9. He then went onto study at the
Convent of St Mark.
The concept of physical dimension, and of
dimensional analysis was introduced by Joseph
Fourier in 1822. The modern concept of dimension
was introduced in 1863 by Clerk James Maxwell,
who synthesized earlier formulations by Fourier.

                                                              Joseph Fourier (1768- 1830)

1.1 Introduction
Think of different phenomena occurring in our nature: formation and disappearance of the
clouds in the sky, appearance of a rainbow, rainfall, evaporation of pond water, strong wind or
storm, cold dry winter, and hot summer. These are examples of physical or natural phenomena.
A clear understanding of such phenomena requires some laws of physics, and these laws are
expressed in terms of physical quantities. Length, time, mass, velocity, force, momentum,
temperature, etc. are examples of physical quantities. The study of physics starts with the
measurement of these diverse physical quantities. Hence, in this chapter, we focus on physical
quantities and the need for their measurement.


Fig 1.1(a) Showing what physics studies                     Fig. 1.1(b) Showing physical phenomena

 Physics is the branch of science and is one of the most fundamental scientific disciplines. The
 main goal of physics is to understand how the universe functions. A scientist who specializes
 in the field of physics is called a physicist.

 The word physics comes from the Latin word physica ('study of nature'), which itself is
 derived from the Greek term φύσις (phúsis ' meaning the origin, nature, property).

 In Sanskrit, physics is called Bhautika, a physical world.

 If a student looks around him/her, he/she finds desks, tables, benches, a board, a projector, a
 duster, and the school building. Beyond it, there are neighboring buildings, trees, vehicles on
 the road, and many more. All of these represent masses. If they are burnt, energy is released.
 The greater the mass, the more will be the energy liberated, and vice-versa. Apart from mass
 and energy, there is nothing around us. Hence, the entire universe is composed of only two
 things; mass and energy. Ultimately, the word ‘physics’ refers to the science of matter and
 energy and their interactions.

 Physics is a quantitative science as it is based on the measurement that comes with numbers.
 Mathematics is used in physics to construct models aimed at predicting natural phenomena.
 Then these predictions are compared to the way the real world works. Physicists continuously
 strive to refine their models so that they can represent the world better. Physics studies very
 large things, as well as very small things. For instance, physicists cannot only study stars,
 planets, and galaxies but also small pieces of matter, such as atoms and electrons. They may
 also study about sound, light, heat, radioactivity, or even space and time. Physics not only
 helps people understand how objects move, but also how they change form, how they make
 sound, how hot or cold they will be, and what they are made of at the microscopic level.
 Physics is the branch of science that deals with the properties of matter and energy along with
 their interaction.

 1.2 Physical Quantity
 A physical quantity is something that can be measured. For example,
 Mass = 87.5 kg, Length = 1.4 m, etc.


Physical quantities can be measured with instruments or can be derived.




                              Fig 1.2 Showing measurement of physical quantity

All the measurable quantities from which the laws of physics are governed are the physical
quantities. When we speak about something, say 2 hours journey, here '2 hours' refers to the
physical quantity of time. Mass, length, time, temperature, velocity, acceleration, pressure,
etc. are physical quantities. To understand them, one must measure and express them
quantitatively in numerical values. This is done using units, which serve as standards of
measurement. Physical quantities are expressed as multiples of these units.
For example, the mass of a bag of apples is 5 kg, the distance is 200km, and the time is 2
hours.
In all these, Physical Quantity = nu, where n is the numerical value of the physical quantity,
and u is the unit of measurement.
Physical quantities are of two types
   1. Fundamental (or Basic) Quantities,
   2. Derived Quantities

Fundamental Quantities
These are the physical quantities that are self-defined and independent of others. Examples
are mass, length, time, temperature, illuminating power, electric current, and amount of a
substance. Moreover, there are two sub-fundamental quantities; a plane angle and a solid
angle.

 These are the quantities that are derived from the fundamental quantities. Examples:

 1.3 Measurement and its need
 In the past, especially at the time of Aristotle, the observations on natural science were
 subjective and the observations varied from one to another because they depended on one’s
 senses. This made communication among physicists difficult. For the description of a
 physical quantity, it should have the system of measurement as per Lord Kelvin (1824 –
 1907), any measurement should be expressed in numerical value for a complete sense.
 Hence otherwise it has no place in physics. An unknown quantity if compared to a known
 reference value is called measurement in physics. The known reference value is called the
 unit.
 Why do we need measurement?

    i) To test the concepts in our hypothesis, we need measurement. The measured
       concepts finally become the variables.


   ii) To understand the phenomenon in physics, one has to perform the experiments. The
        experiments require measurement and one measures several physical properties like
        length, mass, time, temperature, etc
   iii) For the experimental verification of laws and theories, one needs the measurement
        of physical properties.

Concept of measurement:
      Assigning the numerical values to the physical quantities by comparing them with
      their respective units is measurement.

1.4 Unit of a Physical Quantity

As mentioned earlier, a physical quantity should have a system of measurement; it should
be measured and expressed in numbers. The standard of measurement of reference is the
unit.

Conventions in Writing a Unit:

   i) For the unit that is named after a scientist, write the first letter as small letter instead
      of a capital letter.

       For example, we write newton butnot Newton. Similarly, it is written joule but not
       Joule.

   ii) If the unit named after a person is to be written as a symbol, we use a capital letter
       whereas the symbols for other units not fromed from a person's name aren’t written
       in capital letters. For example, N for newton (not n) and m for meter (not M).

   iii) The symbols of units are never expressed in the plural form. We use 5 erg (and not 5
        ergs), 5 kilo (and not 5 kilos), 10 m (but not 10 ms).

   iv) For the symbols of the derived unit, multiplication is joined with a centre dot or a
       non-brake space as N.m or Nm

   v) For the units of derived quantities, the symbols obtained after division are joined using
      solidus or as a negative exponent. For example, metre per second is written as either
      ms-1 or ms-1 . The solidus is used only as one i.e., kg/ms-2 and not as kg/ms-1 -2 .

       However, kgm-1 s2 can also be written in place of kg/ms-2 .

   vi) Symbols must be treated as mathematical entities but not as abbreviations, and they
       do not have an appended period and full stop.

   vii) Full stops aren’t written after the abbreviated units. For example, 50cc 50 ml, but
        not 50 c.c and 50 m. l.


     viii) Names of units are pluralized i.e., henries and not henry. Lux, hertz, and siemens
           are the exceptional cases.

         Since a prefix is a part of unit, it is prepended to the unit symbol without a separator.

         Examples: G in GHz, M in MPa, and k in km.

     ix) Units are of two types; Fundamental unit and derived unit.

     x) 1.4.1 Fundamental and Derived Units

         The units involved in the measurement of fundamental physical quantities are the
         fundamental units.

          The units involved in the measurements of derived physical quantities are the
         derived units.

         The derived units are brought from the fundamental units by simply multiplying or
         dividing two or more fundamental units.

1.4.2 System of Units
At different times in history, and in different parts of the world, people used different sets of
units for measurement. The commonly used systems of units are MKS, CGS and FPS. The
internationally accepted system of units used in science and engineering is called the SI unit.

MKS system:
In this system of measurement, length is measured in metre, mass is measured in kilogram,
and time is measured in second. It was developed in France.

CGS System:
In it, length is measured in centimeter, mass in gram and the time is measured in second. This
system was also developed in France.

FPS System:
In it, length is measured in foot, mass in pound and the time is measured in second. It was
developed in Britain and is known as British system of units.

SI Units:
In 1960, to bring uniformity in measurement in the worldwide sense, the convention of
scientists held in Paris introduced units based on scientific facts, and is now accepted
internationally. This system of units is called SI unit which stands for the Système
international d'unités in the French language.

 atom.

 alloy cylinder with 90% platinum and 10% iridium) kept at the International Bureau of
 Weights and Measures in Paris. It is 4cm high and 4cm in diameter.

1.5     Precision and Significant Figures
Activity 1.1
      i) Stand in front of a dart board and hit the centre of the board with a dart.
      ii) Mark the point the dart hits on the board and repeat the process for several times.
One of the following may be the observation you made.
a) The marked points are neither near the centre nor consistent at anywhere.
b) The marked points are close to each other (consistent) but are regardless of proximity to
   the centre.
c) The marked points of the darts are all closely near the vicinity (or proximity) of the
   centre.
d) All the marked points are near the centre and are consistent.




Fig 1.5 (i) Concepts on Accuracy and Precise Measurement


What are the conclusions from the different observations made above?

Accuracy refers to how close the measurements or observations come to lie at the center of
the targeted point.
Precision refers to how consistent our results of observations are, regardless of closeness to
the centre.
Hence accuracy is the measurement of the observations near the targeted (or true) value
while precision is getting consistent observations. In other words, if the observations are
made near the true value, it gives accuracy. But, the observations consistent to each other
irrespective of the true value give precision. The precision and accuracy can better be
understood with the support of the following




                           Fig 1.5(ii) Concepts on Accuracy and Precise Measurement


In the first fig in 1.5, the observation points are near the true value and consistent, hence it
is the case of accuracy and precision.
 In the second fig in 1.5, there is a consistent result of the observation regardless of the true
target and it is the case of precision.
In the third fig in 1.5, since the measurements are near the true value and inconsistent, it is
the case of accuracy but not precision.
In the fourth fig in 1.5, neither the data are around the near value nor they are consistent, it
is the case of no accuracy and no precision.

A similar activity can be done on a given load. Suppose the loads are said to be 10 kg
backpacks. If several measurements are made near 10kg, such as 9.8kg, 10.2 kg, 10.4 kg;
the case is of accuracy. But if the measurements made are consistent (or close) regardless of
the true value such as 12.5kg, 12.6 kg, and 12.4kg: then it is the case of precision.


A Better Concept to Know:

To understand the real-life example of accuracy and precision, measure the wt. of a 10 kg
mass in the lab and find 3.4 kg, it is not the accurate value of the measurement. If several
other measurements were 3.5 kg, 3.3 kg 3.4 kg and so on, these all represent the precise
measurement. You precisely measure the data but not accurately. However, if the measured
data are at around 10kg as 10.2 kg, 10.1 kg, 9.9 kg, the data all are precise and accurate
too.

1.5.1 Significant Figures:

Significant measure is an art of measuring the physical quantity more accurately and
precisely and hence is important in scientific and technical measures. The larger the number
of significant figures, the greater is the degree of accuracy. The number of significant digits
increases if we measure more precisely with smaller range of uncertainty. The measurement
will have some digits that are certain and one digit is uncertain (or guessed). In understanding
significant figures in measurements, it is important to realize that the precision of a measured
value cannot be more precise than the equipment used for measurement.
Let us take the case that we are measuring the diameter of a ball that is found as 2.64cm.
Here, the digits 2 and 6 are reliable and certain while the last digit '4' is uncertain. Hence the
diameter of the ball has a total 3 significant figures.
Let the measurement for the length of a rod be 3.5 cm. It has a total of 2 significant figures
with 3 as reliable (certain) and the last digit 5 as uncertain. If we find the length as 3.56cm
with some other device, it will be more precise and of more significant figures than 3.5cm. If
the length of the same rod is measured as 3.567 cm using a micrometer screw gauge, it is
more accurate than the former two.
Here are some rules to find the number of significant figures:
i) All the non –zero digits in a given measurement are significant.
i.e. 21.48 has total 4 significant figures


ii)    All the zeros between two non –zero digits are significant but leading zeros are not
   significant.
i.e. 15.0041→ 6 significant figures.
2001 → 4 significant figures.

0015 → 2 significant figures

iii) The zeros to the right of the last non-zero digit are not significant.
 i.e. 9800 → 2 significant figures.
i.e. 050600 → 3 significant figures.
iv)The zeros to the right of the decimal point and before (to the left of) the first non–zero
digits are not significan .They only represent the position of the decimal point.
i.e, 0.006 → 1 significant figure.
0.00025 → 2 significant figures.
0.0080038 → 5 significant figures.
0.25 → 2 significant figures.
v)     The zeros to right of the decimal number are significant only when there is a non-zero
digit on its left
5.00→ 3 significant figure
5.0→ 2 significant figures

0.200→ 3 significant figures

vi) In a measurement expressed in scientific notation, such as N× 10A, the 10A does not
follow the rule of significant figures.
1.6 ×10-19 C → 2 significant figures
6.62 ×10-34 Js → 3 significant figures


 1.5.2 Round off Significant Numbers

 The rounding off of the significant figures is to omit one or more digits from the right side
 of the number until we attain the number of significant figures we want to round it off to.
 For the roundoff, look at the digit on the right end of the number.
 The rules for rounding off are as follows
 a) If the digit to be dropped out is less than 5, the preceding digit remains unchanged on
    rounding off. e.g. 123.42 ≈ 123.4 (in 4 significant numbers)
                              ≈ 123 (in 3 significant number)
 b) If the digit to be dropped out is greater than 5, the preceding digit is increased by 1 in
    rounding off. e.g. 123.167 ≈ 123.17 (in 5 significant numbers)
                              ≈ 124.2 (in 4 significant numbers)
 c) If the digit to be dropped out is exactly 5, the preceding digit to be retained is
 i) Increased by 1 if it is odd. eg. 12.35 ≈ 12.4 (in 3 significant numbers)

 ii) kept unchanged if it is even. eg. 12.45 ≈ 12.4 (in 3 significant

 numbers) 1.5.3 Significant Figures in mathematical operation

 a) In addition, and subtraction:
 When two measurements are added or subtracted one from the other, the answer should
 have the lowest decimal place as that of the input.
 e.g. 3.240 m + 7.14 m = 10.380 m (Incorrect)
                         = 10.38 m (Correct)
And        3.266 m – 2.1 m = 1.166m (Incorrect)
                           = 1.2 m (Correct)


 b) In Multiplication and Division:
 When two measurements are multiplied or divided one by other, the answer should have the
 lowest significant figures as that of the input.
 e.g. 118.6 ×16.2 = 1921.32 (Incorrect)
                   = 1920 or 1.92×103 (Correct, in 3 significant figures)
 118.6 ÷16.2 = 7.3209876543 (Incorrect)
                = 7.32 (Correct, in 3 significant figures)
 125÷ 3 = 41.6666… (Incorrect)
        = 40 (Correct, in 1 significant figure)

1.6     Dimensions of a Physical Quantity
        The concept of dimension of physical quantities was introduced in 1822 by Joseph
        Fourier.
         The dimensions of a physical quantity are the powers that are raised to the
         fundamental quantities involved in a physical quantity.
         In mechanics; mass, length, and time are the three fundamental quantities represented
         respectively as [M], [L], and [T] in dimensional purpose. Temperature is represented
         by [K], electric current is denoted by [A] or [I], and the amount of substance by [N]
         or [mol] . Likewise, the dimensional notation for the luminous intensity is [J] or [cd].
         Hence in a dimensional analysis, the basic quantities with their symbols in a square
         bracketed form for the dimensional analysis are:
         Mass = [M]
         Length = [L]
         Time = [T]
         Temperature = [K]
         Electric current = [A] or [I]
         Amount of substance= [N] or [mol]
         And Luminous Intensity = [J] or [cd]
      Unless mentioned otherwise, the dimensions of a physical quantity X are written as
            X = [Ma Lb Tc]          ……… (i)
         Here [Ma Lb Tc] is the dimensional formula for X and a, b and c are the dimensions
         (power) in mass, length, and time respectively.
         The equation (i) is the dimensional equation for the quantity.
        The square brackets here are read as “dimension of”. One can use either small
       brackets or without the brackets at all, as in M LT -2 . However, it is commonly
       presented within square brackets.

Principle of Homogeneity:

In a valid physical equation, the dimensions of each term on one side must be consistent and
identical to the dimensions of each corresponding term on the other side. This principle is
based on the fact that only the physical quantities of the same kind can be added,
subtracted, or compared. According to this, mass can be added to or subtracted from mass
but not to length. Similarly, force can be added to or subtracted from force but not to
energy.

For example, in the equation v = u + at, dimensional formula of v, u and at are same, and
hence the equation follows the principle of homogeneity.


Types of Physical Quantity
Based on dimension, physical quantities are of the following types:
   a. Dimensional variables: These are physical quantities that do not have a fixed value
       but have dimensions. Examples are work, power, pressure, velocity, etc.
    b. Dimensionless variables: These are physical quantities that possess neither a fixed
           value nor dimensions. Examples are strain, specific gravity, etc. Such quantities
       have no units.
    c. Dimensional Constants: These are the physical quantities that have dimensions and
           a fixed value. Examples are Gravitational constant, Planck’s constant, etc.
    d. Dimensionless constants: These are physical quantities that have no dimension but
       a fixed value. Examples are Coefficient of friction, pi (π), etc.
1.6.1Application of Dimensional Analysis:
Following are the applications of dimensional analysis:
    i)         To check the correctness of a physical relation,
    ii)        To derive a relation between various physical quantities,
    iii)       To convert one system of physical quantity to another system of physical
               quantity
     iv)    To find the dimensions of an unknown physical quantity in a given relation.
Let us discuss some of the applications
To check the correctness of a physical relation:
               1
Let s = ut + 2 at2 be a physical relation.
To test the correctness of this equation whether it is correct or not, let us put the
 dimensional formula of each physical quantity in the relation
[L] = [LT-1 ] [T] + [LT-2 ] [T2 ],
Here ½ is the dimensionless constant and it is needless to write.
Or, [L] = [L] + [L] = [L]
Hence, by the principle of homogeneity of dimension, both sides have the same dimension,
and thus the equation is dimensionally correct.
If the above relation is written as s = ut +at2 and on testing, dimensionally it is found to be
correct as above but the relation is physically wrong as the multiplier ½ in the second term
 is missing.
                                                1
Also, take the physical equation as s= ut2 + 2 at2 . On testing the equation dimensionally, it
is found incorrect, and itis also incorrect physically.
From above it is strongly concluded that a dimensionally correct equation may not be
physically correct. But it is sure that a dimensionally wrong equation is physically wrong.

Vectors




    J. Willard Gibbs (1839-1903)                         Oliver Heaviside (1850-19250)




Vector calculus and its sub-objective Vector Fields was invented by two men J. Willard Gibbs
and Oliver Heaviside at the end of the 19th century. This allowed scientists and mathematicians
to calculate such things as speed and direction from a graph.

J. Willard Gibbs (February 11, 1839 – April 28, 1903) was an American mathematician and
physicist who became an inventor of vector analysis. Josiah Willard Gibbs, born in New Haven,
Connecticut, USA, graduated from Yale (College) in 1858 and continued his career at Yale,
earning his doctorate of philosophy in 1863.

Oliver Heaviside FRS (18 May 1850 – 3 February 1925) was an English self-taught
mathematician and physicist who invented a new technique for solving differential equations
to the Laplace transform, independently developed vector calculus, and rewrote Maxwell's
equations.


2.1 Introduction

Vector, in physics, is a quantity that has both magnitude and direction. It is typically
represented by an arrow whose direction is the same as that of the quantity, and whose length
is proportional to the quantity's magnitude. Although a vector has magnitude and direction,
it does not have position.

Consider the Phenomena:

i) Pokhara lies at a distance of 200 km from Kathmandu. Can a pilot safely land at Pokhara
     after flying 200km just in any direction from Kathmandu?
ii) A screw is rotated in a clockwise direction. What will be its possible direction of
     advancement? Do you anticipate any sense from it?
iii) Imagine your mother asking you to go to a particular shop to get something, will it be
     enough for her to say go 200 m from the main gate? Is this information enough for you
     to locate that shop?
You do realize that it isn't enough, right? You need proper directions, these directions are
themselves vectors and that's why you need vectors.
Physical quantities are classified into two types: scalars and vectors. Scalars, also known as
scalar quantities, are characterized solely by their magnitude. On the other hand, vectors, or
vector quantities, are fully defined by both magnitude and direction.
Mass, length, time, temperature, distance, speed, work, money in the pocket, etc. are scalars.
On the other hand, displacement, velocity, force, etc. are all vectors.
A hundred-rupee defines only magnitude, and thus it is a scalar quantity. The distance of a
place (such as Pokhara lying 200 km from Kathmandu) requires direction for anyone to reach,
making it a vector. The rotation of a screw determines its forward or backward movement,
which involves direction, thus making it a vector quantity.
Moreover, although electric current has both magnitude and direction,it isn’t regarded as a
vector quantity. To qualify as a vector, a physical quantity must possess both magnitude and
direction and adhere to the principles of vector algebra. Hence the electric current, which
does not adhere to the principles of vector algebra, is not considered a vector quantity despite
possessing both magnitude and direction.

a. Scalar and vector Products

Activity 1.3

     i) Take any two natural numbers and multiply them; the result is called a scalar, and the
          multiplication is referred to as the scalar product of the two vectors.
     ii) Take a screw and rotate it clockwise, then note the direction of the advancement.
     iii) Repeat the same process in the anticlockwise direction, and once again note the
          direction of advancement.

         In the first case of screw rotation, it advances downwards, while in the latter case it
         advances upwards, indicating a specific direction in each instance. This product is
         known as the vector product or the cross product of the two vectors.


             The physical significance of both these is actually a beautiful concept.

             For example, in your airplane case, a dot product would give the combined effect of
             the coordinates in different dimensions on each other. A cross product would actually
             help you discover and identify a new path, which would be normal to both the vectors
             you mentioned.

             The cross product could help you identify the path, which would result in the most
             damage if a bird hits the aeroplane through it. The dot product could give you the
             interference of sound waves produced by the revving of an engine on the journey.

             Now, think that while you're in that town, you're suddenly lost at some weird
             intersection. You know that there's a path from the place you came from, A and
             another path to a place, C and all you know is that these roads are at the right angle
             to B, your destination. Take a cross product and voila! You have the road that you
             need to take to get to B before the sun sets and the dinner gets cold.

             As for why the dot product of two vectors is scalar, you just need to brush up on the
             definition of the dot product. It is only when you disregard the directions and consider
             the magnitude (length) of the vectors, multiply them with each other, and then with
             the cosine of angle between them, you get a dot product. There's no direction here.
             Now where would I need it in real life? How about if I want to find out how much
             water is rushing through that little hole in the faucet? I would take the flow of water
             in different outward directions from the hole as vectors and use the dot product to find
             how much of it I am losing.

text:
Kinematics




    Franz Reuleaux                                       Ferdinand Freudenstein

Various physicists and mathematicians including Isaac Newton, Galileo Galilei, and Franz
Reuleaux, contributed to the development of kinematics throughout history. The term
'kinematics' was coined in 1834 by the physicist J.C. Ampère. Since the nature of motion was
not very precisely defined at the time, he felt it necessary to further study it.
German engineering scientist Franz Reuleaux (1829-1905), known as the “father of
kinematics,” conducted extensive studies in the field. He served as a lecturer at the Berlin Royal
Technical Academy and later became its president. Reuleaux was a leader in his profession,
making significant contributions to various domains of science and knowledge.
American physicist and engineer Ferdinand Freudenstein (12 May 1926 – 30 March 2006) is
known as the 'Father of Modern Kinematics.' Freudenstein applied digital computation to the
kinematic synthesis of mechanisms.
.
 3.1 Introduction
 The word “kinematics” comes from the Greek word “kinesis” meaning motion, and is related
 to other English words such as “cinema” (movies) and “kinesiology” (the study of human
 motion). Kinematic analysis is the process of measuring the kinematic quantities used to
 describe motion.
 Kinematics deals with the study of motion without considering its causes. At any given
 instant, a body may be at rest or in motion. If no force acts upon a body, it remains at rest.
 Similarly, if a body is subject to the influence of numerous forces, and their resultant force is
 zero, the body remains at rest.
 Kinematics is used in astrophysics to describe the motion of celestial bodies and systems; and
 in mechanical engineering, robotics and biomechanics to describe the motion of systems


 composed of joined parts (such as an engine, a robotic arm, or the skeleton of the human
 body).
 If a body changes its position with respect to its surroundings over time, it is said to be in
 motion. Conversely, if a body does not change its position with respect to its surroundings,
 it is said to be at rest. Two persons in a moving bus are at rest with respect to each other but
 seem to be in motion when viewed from outside. Similarly, a person or a tree on the surface
 of the Earth appears to be at rest when viewed from outside the Earth due to the Earth's
 motion. Hence, rest and motion are relative terms.

 Some terms on Kinematics
 Distance and Displacement:
 Distance is the total length a particle has traversed during its journey between two points. It
 depends on the shape of the path that a particle follows.
 Displacement, on the other hand, is the shortest distance between the two points in a
 particular direction, and hence it is a vector quantity.
 ● If an ant completes a circle during its journey, the displacement is the length of the
     circumference it traveled, and it returns to the same point, resulting in a zero
     displacement.
 ● A ball thrown upwards falls back to the thrower. The net displacement between the
     initial point (point of throw) and the final point (point of catch) is therefore zero, while
     distance represents the total length covered during the upward and downward motions.
 ● If an object at point P reaches point Q along one zig-zag path and returns to point Q
     following a separate zig-zag path, then the net distance is the sum of the lengths of the
     two zig-zag paths, while displacement is the shortest distance between P and Q.
 ● The magnitude of displacement can be less than distance, as it represents the shortest
     distance in a specific direction.
 ● In one-dimensional motion, distance and displacement can have the same value.

 Speed and Velocity
 Speed is the rate of change of distance, and it is a scalar quantity that can be solved using
 simple ordinary algebra.

Salient Features:
(1)     Since the slope of the velocity vs. time (v-t) graph at every point represents
       acceleration, the graph must be continuous and single-valued to be differentiable.
(2)    Time always increases, so the graph should never trend in the opposite direction of
       the time axis.
(3)    The displacement in a given time interval can be found by calculating the area under
       the curve between two specified time values. It's crucial that the graph is numerically
       integrable, meaning it should not have singularities.
(4)    The graph should never become parallel to v -axis.
(5)    The velocity-time (v-t) graph for motion with uniformly increasing velocity is a
       straight line with a positive slope, while for motion with uniformly decreasing
       velocity, it is a straight line with a negative slope.
(6)    The velocity-time (v-t) graph of a body with increasing/decreasing acceleration is a
       curve that exhibits a continuously increasing/decreasing slope as time progresses.

text:
Dynamics

The foundations of dynamics were laid at the end of the 16th century by Galileo, who, by
experimenting with a smooth ball rolling down an inclined plane, derived the law of motion
for falling bodies; he was also the first to recognize that force is the cause of changes in the
velocity of a body.
Isaac Newton was the first to formulate the fundamental physical laws that govern dynamics
in classical non-relativistic physics, especially his second law of motion.
Isaac Newton is responsible for the precise formulation of the laws of motion, describing how
speed and position vary over a short period of time.




        Galileo (Feb 15, 1564 – Jan 8, 1642)




4.1 Introduction
 Dynamics is a branch of mechanics that deals with the study of the motion of an object by
 taking its cause.

 4.1.1 Force:
 Activity 4.1
 Do the following activities and answer the questions that follow:
        i) As soon as your class ends, arrange the teaching materials such as the duster and
             markers on the table and leave the class.
        ii) Notice the states of those materials on the following day after you enter the class.
        iii) If you find the states of the body intact, can you guess what’s going on?
        iv) If you see the states of the body disturbed, write your guess on what the
             disturbing agents might be.


 Certainly, when one finds something disturbed in the state, one concludes that an external
 agent must have either pushed or pulled the objects and disturbed them. This external agent
 is called the force.
 Hence, the force is an external agency that causes a change in the state of a body.
 4.1.2 Inertia
 Every object has a tendency to continue in the state it is in, i.e. objects resist the change in their
 state. This resistance of a body to change its state is called inertia. Inertia is directly proportional to
 its mass. Therefore, the greater the mass, the greater the inertia, which is expressed by the equation I
    m where I represents inertia and m represents mass.
 Examples:
    i) Suppose there are two water buckets on the ground, one filled with water and the
         other empty. If a strong wind blows, the empty bucket gets disturbed, while the
         water-filled bucket remains in the same state. This is due to the greater inertia of the
         water-filled bucket because of greater mass. It exhibits greater resistance and remains
         at rest.
    ii) If a solid iron ball and a hollow rubber ball, both of the same size, are rolling towards
         you, you will find it easier to stop the hollow one. This is due to its lower mass and
         less inertia.
 Inertia has the following types:
 Inertia of rest: When the bus driver suddenly accelerates the bus, the passengers in the bus
 lean backward. This is because they possess the inertia of rest.
 Inertia of motion: When a moving bus suddenly stops, passengers lean forward due to the
 inertia of motion.
 Inertia of direction: A moving bus, when suddenly turns left or right, the passengers lean
 right or left respectively. It’s because of the inertia of direction, i.e. their resistance to
 change in direction.
       1.1.3 Linear Momentum and Impulse:

Linear Momentum: It describes the motion of a body and is quantified by the product of its
mass and velocity. The formula for momentum is given by:

Momentum = mass×velocity

Or, p = mv

Clearly, change in momentum of a body is due to the change in velocity. A change in velocity,
in turn, implies acceleration. A body of mass m hence has some force F acted upon it, and
hence the change in momentum is the force according to Newton.

  Impulse:
Do the activities that follow.
i) You slapped a baby’s face.
ii) You slipped on a road and
iii) Two vehicles suddenly collided.
     Consider the common factors among these three events. What result would follow after
     these occurrences?


    Certainly, the result of these three events is what we know as impulse. In all of these
    events, two common factors are involved: a significant force and a short duration. None
    of these actions—slapping, slipping, or collision—lasts for an extended period.
    The effect of a significant force applied for a short duration of time on a body is known as
    impulse. Mathematically, impulse is calculated as the product of force and time,
    expressed as F. ∆t
    i.e., impulse = F.∆𝑡

According to Newton’s second law of motion, force is defined as the rate of change in the
momentum.
i.e, F = mv−mu = m( v−u )
           ∆t        ∆t
Or, F. ∆t = mv – mu
∴ Impulse = momentum change.
 Hence, impulse results in a change in the momentum of a body.
 -When a running man slips, he can’t continue his motion, leading to a change in
    momentum. Similarly, when a ball is struck, it exhibits a change in motion, which
    corresponds to a change in its momentum.
 -Likewise, when two cars collide, they alter their motion, resulting in a change in
 momentum.
 Hence the effect of the impulse is to bring a change in the momentum. The fact that impulse
 is equal to the change in momentum is called as impulse- momentum theorem.
 More Examples:

     While catching a falling ball, one lowers his hand, which increases the time of impact,
     thereby reducing the force to minimize injury.
     i) If we fall on a rock or a cemented floor, we come to an immediate stop, thereby
     increasing the force of impact, which causes more harm.
     ii) China wares and glass wares are wrapped in paper to increase the time of impact,
     thereby reducing the force and protecting the items.

= 5.25 – (-7.5)
= 12.75 kg ms-1 = Impulse (Impulse- Momentum theory)

     1.2 Principle of Conservation of Linear Momentum
 In the realm of dynamics, the principle of conservation of momentum asserts that within a
 system comprising two colliding bodies, the aggregate momentum remains constant
 provided no external forces exert their influence on the system. This fundamental concept
 states that the combined momentum of two bodies before a collision equals the total
 momentum after the collision. This conservation of momentum arises from the absence of
 external forces, ensuring that initial and final momentum values remain identical.
 Statement: For a system of two colliding bodies, the total momentum before the collision is
 equal to the total momentum after the collision if no external force acts on the system.
 Let us consider two bodies X and Y of masses m1 and m2 moving initially with velocities
 u1 and u2 respectively in a direction such that u1 > u2 .

         same direction such that v2 > v1 .

1. 3 Newton’s Laws of Motion

 In the exploration of particle motion, Sir Isaac Newton meticulously employed the scientific
 method to derive three foundational principles, famously recognized as Newton's Laws of
 Motion. These laws serve as the bedrock of classical mechanics, encapsulating the
 fundamental dynamics governing the behavior of objects in motion. The trio comprises the
 First Law of Motion, which delineates the inertia-based nature of objects; the Second Law of


Motion, explicating the relationship between force, mass, and acceleration; and the Third
Law of Motion, illuminating the reciprocal action and reaction between interacting bodies.
These laws collectively form an interconnected framework, providing a comprehensive

4.3.1 Newton’s First Law of Motion:
    Force is involved during changes in the state of your body. Unless there is a change in
    your state, no force is necessary, and you remain intact. In other words, force is
    required to change direction, come to rest, start motion, accelerate, or decelerate. If no
    force is applied during such changes, you remain in your original state.
    Sir Isaac Newton studied these phenomena in the motion of bodies and formulated a
    law known as Newton’s first law of motion.

Statement: Everybody remains in its own state unless an external force is acted upon.
According to it, a body at rest will remain at rest, and a body in motion will continue
moving with the same speed along a straight line unless acted upon by an external force. To
change from rest to motion, or vice versa, to accelerate, decelerate, or change direction, an
external agency, called force, is required.
 If the force isn’t acted, the body remains in its own state i.e, either at rest or in motion in a
straight line.

Since the force appears as a role model to change the state of the body in the first law, the
first law hence defines the force.
The law is also known as the law of inertia because a body remains inert unless acted
upon by a force. This property exhibited by the body is called inertia, hence the term 'law
of inertia'.

Examples:
   i)     When a bus at rest suddenly begins to move, the passengers lean backwards.
          According to the first law of motion, a force is exerted on the bus, causing it to
          move forward. However, the upper part of the passengers, not directly affected
          by the force, exhibit the property of inertia of rest. As a result, the passengers
          lean backwards.
   ii)    When a moving bus suddenly stops, the passengers lean forward due to the
          inertia of motion, or as per the first law, a force acts on the bus causing it to
          come to a stop with the lower parts of the passengers attached to their seats.
          However, due to the absence of a force acting on the passengers directly, they
          tend to remain in motion and thus lean backward.
   iii)   When a moving bus suddenly turns into a direction, the passengers lean in the
          opposite direction. This is due to the inertia of direction, or according to the first
          law, because no force is acting directly on the passengers. As the passengers
          continue their motion in the same straight line, they oppose the change in
          direction and consequently lean in the opposite direction.
   iv)    Mangoes fall on shaking the mango tree.
   v)      One takes a short run before jumping.


       vi)           If in an emergency, we need to jump off a moving bus while jumping off, an
                     external force is applied to our legs (or feet), causing them to reach the targeted
                     point, while no force is exerted on the upper part of the body. Consequently, the
                     upper part of the body, continuing with the motion of the bus, tends to fall in the
                     direction of the bus. Therefore, for a safe jump, one should jump in the direction
                     of the moving bus.
       vii)          A moving fan goes on slowing down and finally stops. It doesn’t violate the first
                     law.
       viii)         A rolling ball on the ground goes on slowing down and finally stops. It also
                     doesn’t violate the first law.

      If a body under the action of forces is at rest, the body is said to be in equilibrium.

  A group of forces that all act at the same point are called concurrent forces. If the resultant
  of these concurrent forces acting at a point on a body is zero, the body is said to be in
  equilibrium.

text:
Work, Energy & Power
The French mathematician Gaspard-Gustave Coriolis introduced the term work in 1826
saying "weight lifted through a height", similar to the case of early steam engines to lift
buckets of water out of flooded ore mines. The modern statement: "work is force times path"
is due to him and gave the correct formula for change in kinetic energy associated with work
although he spoke of force vive (including the modern factor ½), instead of kinetic energy.
The word energy is derived from the Greek word ἐνέργεια (energeia) which appears for the
first time in the 4th century BCE works of Aristotal.
 Leibniz defined the product of the mass of an object and its velocity squared from the idea of
Vis viva (living force), as a modern concept of the energy.
In 1802 lectures to the Royal Society, Thomas Young was the first to use the term energy in
its modern sense, instead of Vis viva. The term finally was first invented by him in 1807 after
the Greek word Energeia that roughly translates to “activity.” Energy is the ability for an
object to perform work on another object”.
Moreover, Gustave-Gaspard Coriolis described the term kinetic energy in 1829 in its modern
sense, and Thomas Rankine introduced the term potential energy in 1853.




Gaspard-Gustave Coriolis(1792-1843)                              Thomas Young(1773-1829)

Learning Outcomes

5.1 Introduction

 Do or observe the following tasks:
         i) Visit a bank or some company, or some industrial area, and notice a guard
              standing at the gate.
         ii) Visit the fields and watch a farmer digging or ploughing the field.
         iii) Note some people carrying loads on their backs.


         iv) Watch a man lifting a bucket of water and walking along the road.
         v) Observe a man with loads on his head and walking along.
         vi) Remember, the people involved in all these tasks receive payment accordingly.
Q: Do all these phenomena refer to a specific type of work? If they all imply the act of doing
something, what is the definition of this work? In case the nature of the work varies, how
would you define work to encompass all these tasks?

In a common sense, all of these tasks exemplify work. However, in physics, the concept of
work carries a distinct meaning. Work is defined as the product of a force acting upon a
system and the displacement of that system occurring in the direction of the force.
Mathematically, work (w) = force (f).displacement (d)
i.e, w= f.d
If the force acts at an angle θ, then w = fdcosθ
         For d =0, w = 0
Hence for work to occur, there must be displacement in the direction of the force. If
the displacement is zero, no work is done. Therefore,
i) A gateman or guard standing all day is often considered as doing no work, as there is no
     net displacement.
ii) A man carrying a load while standing also does not perform any work.
iii) Additionally, the work done by static friction exerted by a body on a surface is zero
     because there is no displacement.

         If θ =00 , w = fd i.e, they act in the same direction.
         If θ = 900 , w = 0
iv) A man walking while carrying a water bucket does zero work because the load acts
      vertically downwards while he moves forward. In this case, the load and the
      displacement are perpendicular, forming a 90-degree angle. According to the formula w
      = fdcosθ, where θ represents the angle between force and displacement, the cosine of
      90 degrees is 0, resulting in zero work being done.
v) The work done by the centripetal force around a circle is zero because the force and the
      displacement act at 90 degrees.
vi) The work done by the tension in a string when a body undergoes a circular path is also
      zero.
vii) A coolie carrying a load on his head while traveling on a platform is said to have done
      zero work.
viii) The work done due to the movement of a body on a frictionless surface, when the force
      (F) is equal to zero, is also zero.
     But, a porter moving vertically up the stairs with a suitcase on his head does work.
     Why?
     → The porter applies the force upwards against the load that is acting vertically
     downwards. Since the displacement here is in the direction of the force applied by the
     porter, there is work done.


      Units and Dimension of Work:
        1 joule=?
        It is the work done by a force of 1N to produce 1m displacement.
        i.e, 1 joule = 1N ×1m. The joule refers to the name of James, an English physicist.
        SI Units: kilogram weight meter (or kilogram force meter⇒ kg wt m (or kgf m)
        And 1 kgf m = 9.8 joule meter
     For the dimensional formula for work, W = Fdcosθ= [M LT-2 ] × [L] = [ML2 T-2 ] × [L] =
     [M L2 T-2 ]

a.    Work Done by a Constant Force:

      If a force is applied on a system or on a particle, and displacement is caused in the
      direction of the force, then work done, W = Fd
      If the force makes an angle θ with the displacement, we consider the effective part of
      the force in the direction of the displacement, known as the component of the force
      Fcosθ. Therefore, the work done, W, is calculated as W = Fcosθd = Fdcosθ. Hence W =
      Fd cosθ is the general formula.
      If θ = 0, then W = Fd i.e F and d act in the same direction.
      If θ = 900 , then W = 0 as cos900 = 0
      Up to this point, the examples we have studied are all the instances of work done by a
      constant force.




        Fig 5.1: A concept of work
      And for such a constant force, w= F.d
      If the force acts at an angle θ, then w = Fdcosθ.

     Work done by a body: This refers to the work done by the body on its surroundings,
         often resulting in a decrease in its energy (e.g., kinetic energy).
     Work done on a body: This refers to the work done on the body by an external force,
         often resulting in an increase in its energy (e.g., potential energy).
     Work done by a body is the energy lost by the body and hence the work done is

 5.4 Power
Power is defined as the rate at which work is done or energy is transferred over time. It
quantifies how quickly energy is used or converted from one form to another.
Mathematically, Power= work done/ time taken.

  The standard unit of power is watt (W), where 1 watt is 1 joule of work done in 1 s. It is
 after the Scottish physicist James Watt, an inventor of the steam engine, the unit is used.
Power can also be expressed in different contexts, such as electrical power, where it is
defined as the product of voltage V and current I:
Horse power is another unit for power used earlier specially in power of vehicle.
     And 1 horse Power (H.P) = 746 watt.

     5.5 Energy
     Energy is the capacity to do work. If work is performed, energy is expended, and if
     energy is gained, an equivalent amount of work has been done.
     There are many kinds of energy, with the main category being the division of energy
     into mechanical energy and non-mechanical energy. Non-mechanical energies include
     heat energy, sound energy, light energy, nuclear energy, etc. Here, we will discuss
     mechanical energy, which is divided into two categories: kinetic energy and potential
     energy. This distinction between mechanical and non-mechanical energy, as well as the
     categorization of mechanical energy into kinetic and potential energy, aligns with
     fundamental concepts in physics. Let's explore this breakdown further.
     5.5.1 Mechanical Energy:

   Kinetic energy:
    Imagine the following phenomena:
           i. You are sitting on the ground at some distance from your child (your nephew),
           who is playing nearby. You are suddenly informed that the child is playing with
           an explosive ball that is going to explode within a few minutes. What do you do
           then?


               You run as fast as you can to save the child from the possible danger. All the
               energy within you is used up in running fast. This total energy within you is what
               we call Kinetic Energy.
               ii. You took part in a district-level race competition organized by your college.
               How did you run during your turn in the competition? Can you describe it? You
               definitely answer that you ran as fast as you could. Indeed, all the energy you
               possessed was converted into kinetic energy due to such a terrific race.

5.6 Principle of Conservation of Energy
  We have studied different forms of energy in our previous classes. These include
  mechanical energy, heat energy, sound energy, chemical energy, light energy, electrical
  energy, and so on.
  When one form of energy disappears, the next form of energy is evolved, and vice versa.
  There is no destruction or creation of energy; it only changes its form.


i) When we turn on a radio, the chemical energy in the battery or the electrical energy
    supplied is converted into sound energy. Here, the loss of the former type of energy is
    balanced by the production of the second kind of energy.
ii) When a fan is turned on, the electrical energy supplied is converted into mechanical
    energy. The amount of electrical energy expended is balanced by the generation of
    mechanical energy.

     In summary, the principle of conservation of energy can be stated as:
      “Energy can neither be created nor be destroyed, but it can be changed from one form
     to another form”
iii) The principle of conservation of energy is an empirical principle and cannot be proved
    purely through mathematics.
iv) The law is also believed to be universally valid, as it has not been contradicted in any
    experiment or observation of nature.
v) The law connects mechanics to all other branches of physics, making the concept of
    energy one of the unifying ideas of physics.
vi) The mechanical energy is conserved only when the forces are conservative in nature.
vii) The energy spent against the friction dissipates in the form of heat energy which isn’t
     available for useful work.

    The conservation of energy is best understood by taking the example of a pendulum
    motion.

5.6.1 Principle of Conservation of Mechanical Energy (falling body case)

In the case of a falling body, assuming air resistance is negligible (so that only gravitational

Statement: Energy can neither be created nor be destroyed, but it can be changed from one
form to another form.
                                OR


The total mechanical energy of an isolated system remains conserved.

5.7 Conservative and Non- conservative Forces

5.7.1 Conservative force:
It is the force under the action of which total mechanical energy remains conserved.
Gravitational force, elastic force, magnetic force, electrostatic force, and all the field forces
are examples of the conservative force. A conservative force has the following properties:
i) It is independent of the path, but depends on the initial and the final position of the
     body.




          Fig 5.9: Showing the nature of conservative force

ii) Work done by a conservative force around a closed path is zero.
iii) Work done by it is completely recoverable and is central in nature.
iv) Conservative forces permit one to write elegant conservation laws, such as the
    conservation of mechanical energy.
                          Ef = Ei


 5.7.2 Non- Conservative Force:
 It is the force under the action of which total mechanical energy isn’t conserved. This is
 because a part of the energy is dissipated in the form of sound, heat, etc. Frictional forces,
 tension forces, push and pull actions, applied forces, and viscous forces are examples of
 non-conservative forces. A non-conservative force has the following properties:
 i) It is path-dependent force. More work will be done on a longer path.
 ii) The work done by a non-conservative force around a closed path is not zero. For
      example, consider going from home to college and back. The work done in both the
      paths is against friction and differs, resulting in a non-zero value of the work done. The
      longer the path, the more work friction does.
 iii) Work done by it isn’t completely recoverable and is retarding in nature.
 iv) The non-conservative forces disrupt the fundamental conservation laws, such as the
      conservation of mechanical energy
                               Ef < Ei
 Unless one adds the explicit factor for work, they do:

                           Ef = Ei + W
 One can improve the law of conservation of mechanical energy to work in real-world
 situations by accounting for friction:
      KEf +GPEf = KEi + GPEi +Wf, Wf→ work done by friction.

 5.8 Collision; Elastic and Inelastic Collision

     In physics, the term "collision" typically implies an interaction between two or more
     objects where they exert forces on each other, resulting in a change in their motion. While
     physical contact is the most common scenario in collisions, it is not strictly necessary for
     a collision to occur. For example, the collision of α-particles with the nucleus involves no
     physical contact, whereas the collision between two billiard balls or a cricket ball and a
     bat does.

     Though most common examples of collisions involve physical contact, it is true that, in
     a broader sense, a collision can occur without direct physical contact if there is an
     interaction through forces such as gravitational or electromagnetic forces, leading to a
     change in motion. However, in everyday usage and most introductory physics contexts,
     collisions are typically associated with physical contact.

     During a collision, the total energy and momentum of the system of colliding objects
     remain conserved.


      Fig 5.14: Showing how α- particles collide with nucleus.

 Coefficient of Restitution
 For any two colliding bodies, the ratio of the relative velocity after the collision to the
 relative velocity before the collision is called the coefficient of restitution.
 i.e., Coefficient of Restitution, e = Relative velocity after collision/Relative velocity
 before collision.
 The value of e lies as 0 <e <1, e = 1
  for perfectly elastic collision. e = 0,
  for perfectly inelastic collision.

text:
Circular Motion

Think of circular motion as the result of a balance between two
forces–one centrifugal, the other centripetal (toward the
center)–rather than as the result of one force, a centripetal
force, which constantly deflects the body away from its inertial
path in a straight line. Newton extended the dynamics of
intermittent colliding bodies to his analysis of bodies subject to
a continuous force. He determined the nature of the force
directed toward the center of a circle that will move the body
uniformly around the circle (i.e., the solution to the direct
problem of uniform circular motion). In this analysis, the
                                                                     Sir Isaac Newton (1642-1726)
circular path is approximated by a polygonal path of n sides,
where the number of sides of the polygon will ultimately
increase without limit. As the number of sides of the polygon
was increased, the polygonal path approached a circular path.

6.1 Introduction to Circular Motion

Let's engage in the activity to gain an understanding of circular motion:
Activity 6.1
i) Take a ball or a stone weighing approximately 100 grams and tie it with an inextensible
    string.
ii) Hold one end of the rope and allow it to move in a circular path.
iii) Try to identify the force on the stone and the rope separately with the help of your
     teacher.
iv) Guess the velocity if the rope breaks at A, B, C and D as indicated in the figure.
v) Find the change in velocity of the ball between the points A and B, A and C and C and
     D if |V A| = |V B| = |V C| = |V D| = 5ms-1 .




                                       Fig 6.1: Circular motion


    A body is said to be in a circular motion if it remains at an equidistance from a fixed point.
    This fixed point is called the center of the circular path, and the distance is known as the
    radius vector.
    In circular motion, there is a change in velocity at every point along the path. The
    velocity at each point is given by the tangent drawn at that point.
    One writes,
    Velocity = magnitude + direction
              = speed + direction.
    At each point, there is a change in the direction of the motion. Therefore, the change in
    velocity is due to the change in direction.
Since there is a change in velocity, acceleration is present, and thus any object undergoing
circular motion experiences a force. The force directed towards the center is called the
centripetal force, while the force directed away from the center is sometimes referred to as
the centrifugal force. However, it's important to note that centrifugal force is more accurately
described as a pseudo-force resulting from the inertia of the object. Both forces have equal
magnitudes but are directed oppositely.
A body moving at a constant speed in circular motion has no net work done on it.




        Fig 6.2: Concept on centripetal and centrifugal force.

    Examples:

         i) If you whirl a bucket with some water in it in a vertical circle, the water doesn’t
              fall down due to the centrifugal force that pushes it away from the centre,
              which is balanced by the inwards centripetal force.
         ii) While travelling in a bus we lean outwards when the bus undergoes a circular
              path due to the centrifugal force that finally is balanced by the inwards
              centripetal force.
         iii) When a small piece of stone tied to a string is whirled in a circular path, the
              stone tries to go away by detaching the string due to the action of the
              centrifugal force and the string is pulling the stone towards the centre due to
              the centripetal force.
         iv) Mud flying off a tire is an example of centrifugal force, while a satellite
              orbiting the Earth is an example of centripetal force.


         v) Due to the Earth's orbiting motion, it experiences centrifugal force, resulting in
            flattening at the poles and bulging at the equator.

6.3 Centripetal Acceleration
Since there is a change in velocity in a circular motion, there is some acceleration present that

compensated for by the centrifugal force.

6.7 Application of Centripetal Force
The application of centripetal force mainly focuses on the automobiles while making a turn,
the turn is an arc of a circular path and the friction on the wheels provides the necessary
centripetal force to balance the motion.

of the curve.

Some Facts on Circular Motion
So far we have studied circular motion, there are three mathematical quantities i.e. Speed,
Acceleration and Force as a primary matter of interest to analyze a circular motion.


A repetitive closed motion is generally not allowed as a perfect circle. Hence the motion in a
circle is very important in our daily life such as moon’s revolution around the Earth, Earth’s
revolution around the sun, electron orbital motion round the nucleus, satellites going round the
Earth and the mechanism of centrifuge used to segregate the unwanted impurities.
The angular displacement in a circular motion denoted by θ whose unit is radian is a vector
                      𝑙
quantity because θ = 𝑟.
The direction of the angular displacement is given by the right-hand rule, according to which
if the curled fingers represent the direction of motion, the thumb held perpendicular to the
curvature of the fingers represents the direction of the angular displacement. Hence, by
analyzing the same sense of the right-hand rule, the angular velocity has the direction of the
thumb. For counterclockwise rotation, ω directs upwards, while it directs downwards for
clockwise rotation.
 According to Newton’s first law of motion, a body can't change its direction itself without
force. However, in circular motion, the change is due to the centripetal force. The body tries to
gain its natural linear path, giving rise to what is called the centrifugal force. Hence, this is the
reason why centripetal and centrifugal forces are equal but opposite in nature, respectively
representing the forces of action and reaction. In cases of non-uniform circular motion,
accelerations are defined in both the radial and tangential directions.
A body undergoing circular motion with increasing angular velocity experiences both
centripetal and tangential accelerations resulting in a net acceleration.

text:
Gravitation


Numerous theories of gravitation emerged in ancient Greek
philosophy and were further elaborated upon through the
Middle Ages by scientists from various parts of the world.
These ideas gained significant momentum during the
Renaissance and Scientific Revolution, ultimately
culminating in the formulation of Newton's law of gravity.
Sir Isaac Newton discovered the existence of gravity. It is
said that he realised about gravity when he saw an apple fall
down from a tree. Newton came up with the idea that some
unseen force must attract the apple towards the Earth. He
named this force “gravity” from the Latin word “gravitas”,
meaning “weight”. Finally in series of his work, Newton
came to establish a famous law of gravitation, now called as
Newton’s universal law of gravitation and it is his most
renowned work.



     Newton’s law of gravitation

     7.1 Introduction:
        Before understanding the insight of the chapter, let’s observe an activity.
        Observe the following phenomena.
     i) The Earth is holding itself and rotating while the atmosphere surrounds it.
     ii) Binding the Earth and the other planets, along with the perennial source of energy, the sun

Center of Gravity:
It is the point through which the resultant weight of the body is supposed to be acting
vertically downwards. The center of gravity of an object is a geometric property representing
the average location of the body's weight. The center of gravity (C.G) may or may not lie
within the body. For a spherical or disk-like body, it lies at the center within the material of


the body. However, for a ring or spherical enclosure, the C.G also lies at the center but not
within the material of the body.
The center of gravity is used in designing static structures such as buildings, bridges, flying
airplanes, kites, etc. If the center of gravity lies in the middle and at a lower position, it
provides more stability to the structure.

   What was the resultant motion of the star during this period of observation?
The star you observe consistently appears directly above the zenith. The Earth completes a
cycle in a total time of 24 hours.
The fact that the star maintains the same position every 24 hours indicates that it follows the
same motion as the Earth, with the same time period. This makes the star appear stationary
when viewed from the Earth.
Therefore, in each instance, you perceive the star as if it were at rest, akin to a car in a park,
and hence the name given to the orbit as a parking orbit or the geostationary orbit.
A geostationary orbit or a parking orbit has the same time period as that of the Earth and
is known as a synchronous orbit with T = 24 hours. A satellite revolving in such a parking
orbit with T = 24 hours is called a geostationary satellite or a synchronous satellite. Such
satellites are used in telecommunications, weather forecasting, and live video transmission
from one part of the Earth to another.

 The orbiting spacecraft is in the gravitational field of the Earth that experiences an

7.13 Global Positioning System (GPS)
Satellite-based navigation is utilized to synchronize location, velocity, and time while traveling
by air, sea, or land. Similar fields that utilize GPS include military operations, surveying,
aviation, road transportation, and smartphones.
The GPS, or Global Positioning System, is a global navigation satellite system consisting of a
receiver and a constellation of 24 satellites distributed across six Earth-centered orbital planes,


with each plane hosting four satellites. These satellites orbit at an altitude of about 20,000 km
above the Earth at a speed of 14,000 km/h.
To determine a location on the Earth’s surface, GPS requires signals from three satellites. A
fourth satellite is then used to validate the information obtained from the other three. This
additional satellite enables GPS to provide altitude information, thus moving us into the third
dimension. GPS operates using a technique known as trilateration or triangulation. Trilateration
utilizes signals to calculate location, velocity, and elevation, while triangulation is employed to
measure angles rather than distances.
Satellites transmit signals to GPS devices on or near the Earth's surface, and a device must be
capable of receiving signals from at least four satellites to calculate its location.
Each satellite orbits the Earth twice a day, transmitting a unique signal along with orbital
parameters and time information. A GPS system can receive signals from six or more satellites.
A GPS device captures microwave signals from satellites to determine the distance between
the satellite and the GPS system. However, since GPS provides only distance information, it
alone cannot provide precise location data.
A single satellite sends a signal, creating a circle. The second satellite creates another circle,
narrowing down the location to one of two points where the circles intersect. With the third
satellite, the location is determined as the device lies at the intersection point of the three circles.
However, our world is three-dimensional in nature. Satellites generate spheres instead of
circles, resulting in two points of intersection for the three spheres from the three satellites.
Finally, the point nearest to the Earth's surface is chosen as the location.




  Fig7.20: Global Position of the GPS with 3 satellite Arrangement


As GPS moves, the radius, which is the distance from the two satellites, changes, thereby
generating new spheres that provide updated positions.
GPS operates continuously, regardless of weather conditions. Hence, it is a powerful and
dependable tool in various industries and other areas of business and organizations. Pilots,
boat captains, surveyors, scientists, and workers rely on GPS information in their daily work.
It is used for preparing accurate surveys and maps, conducting precise time measurements,
and tracking positions or locations
Uses of GPS:
            i)     Location findings
            ii)    Navigation ( or finding of another location from a given location)
            iii)   Tracking ( For an object's or a person's movement)
            iv)    Mapping of the world.
            v)     Timing for the precise measurement
Factors Affecting GPS Accuracy:
Following are the key factors that affect the GPS accuracy:
           i) Atmospheric conditions: solar storms, heavy storm cover and ionospheric
                delays disturb the GPS system.
           ii) Physical conditions: High altitude mountainous regions, trees and tall
                buildings disturb the signals passage time.
           iii) Calculation Error: It occurs from the device’s hardware.
           iv) Ephemeris: It occurs due to the incorrect orbital model within the satellite.
Components of GPS System:
It consists of mainly three segments:
                   Space (satellite segment): The 24-satellite orbiting twice a day transmit
                   signals to users on the Earth with timing.
                   Control Segment: It includes tracking and operating the satellite in space
                   and monitoring transmissions. For this, 5 monitoring stations are kept
                   almost in all the continent with North and South America combined.
                   Qualified signals are sent to the master control stations. In case of defects
                   in signals, hey are sent back to the GPS satellite. FIG
                   User equipment (user segment); GPS receivers and transmitters collect
                   and process signals from the GPS satellites and determine distance. The
                   measurement accuracy increases with the number of satellites.

GPS vs GNSS; The Difference:

GPS is one of several satellite constellations, while GNSS describes all satellite constellations
in orbit. GNSS is formed by combining multiple constellations. The accuracy of positioning
technology depends on these various constellations.

text:
Elasticity

  Robert Hooke [Born on July 18 (July 28, New Style), 1635,
  Freshwater, Isle England], is an English physicist who
  discovered the law of elasticity, known as Hooke’s law.
  In 1655 Hooke was employed by Robert Boyle to construct
  the Boylean air pump. Five years later, Hooke discovered his
  law of elasticity, which states that the stretching of a solid
  body (e.g., metal wood) is proportional to the force applied to
  it. The law laid the basis for studies of stress and strain and
  for understanding of elastic materials. He applied these            Fig: Robert Hooke
  studies in his designs for the balance springs of watches; his
  interest in timekeeping was further reflected in his effort to
  improve the pendulum for clock regulation. Robert Hooke has
  (1660) developed a mathematical relationship between
  tension and extension. In 1660, he discovered the law of
  elasticity which states the stretching of a solid is proportional
  to the force applied. Poison, Cauchy and G Stoke showed the
  equation of the general theory of elasticity. In 1662 he was
  appointed curator of experiments to the Royal
  Society of London and was elected a fellow the following
  year.


8.1 Introduction
 Activity 8.1
 Do the activities that follows:




                           Fig 8.1: Showing the elastic behavior


 i) Take a metallic (or a hard rubber) spring with a small marble attached at the free ends
      and, place it on a table.
 ii) Bring the marbles close to each other and then release them. Observe what happens
      next.
 iii) Pull the marbles away from each other and release them again. Observe what happens.
      Think for yourself and collect more ideas on what‘s going on there.
The force given in either case is the deforming force that changes the configuration of the
body. When the deforming force in either case is removed, the body regains its original
configuration. In doing so, there is a force setting up internally, called the restoring force.
When the deforming force employed to extend the spring is large enough, the body can’t
regain its original configuration. Such a stage is the stage of plasticity, and the body is said to
be in a plastic stage (or in a damaged state in some context of engineering and structural
analysis). When a body regains its original configuration, it is in the elastic stage, and the
phenomenon is elasticity.
Hence elasticity is the property of a matter by virtue of which it regains its original shape
and size after the removal of the deforming force.
In physics, the more the rigidity, the more is the elasticity.
Hence this is why iron is said to be more elastic than rubber.
  In the same sense, a solid is more elastic than a liquid and the liquid is more elastic than
gases. The origin of elasticity is due to the presence of short-range molecular interaction
inside the matter.
Every matter is made of atoms and molecules. The separation of such particles in a normal
state is ro . If the material is elongated using a deforming force, the separation ro increases, and
an attractive force between the particles comes into play, returning it to its original
configuration. If the body is contracted, ro decreases, and a repulsive force establishes itself,
capable of returning it to its original configuration.
If the deforming force is so large that the distance between the particles is much greater
 than ro , the two particles cannot attract each other, and the body is in the plastic stage.
Hence, the point of the deforming force at which the body regains its original configuration
is the elastic limit. Beyond this point, the body is in the plastic stage (or damaged in the case
considered).

 Elasticity:
 As already mentioned, elasticity is the property of matter by virtue of which it regains its
 original shape and size after the removal of the deforming force.
 If the body completely regains its original configuration immediately after the removal of
 the deforming force, then the body is said to be perfectly elastic body.
 This is only the ideal assumption. Quartz and phosphor bronze approach this assumption.


Plasticity:




   Fig 8.9: Stress vs Strain curve Showing plasticity
A perfectly plastic body is one that does not regain its original configuration at all after the
removal of the deforming force, regardless of the magnitude of the force applied. Examples
of such materials include paraffin wax, putty, and wet clay.
Applications of Elasticity
i) A thick metallic rope used in a crane is employed to lift the maximum load, which should
     not exceed the elastic limit of the rope's material. By understanding this elastic limit and
     the extension per unit length of the material, one can determine the required area of the
     wire's cross-section.
ii) Elasticity is used in estimating the altitude of a mountain. Elasticity principles, such as
     atmospheric pressure changes, can indirectly influence altitude measurements.
iii) When designing a bridge, we must consider elasticity along with factors such as traffic
     load, bridge weight, wind force, and others. The bridge is designed to ensure it neither
     bends excessively nor breaks under various conditions.

Elastic limit:
The elastic limit, denoted as E, is the upper limit beyond which a body loses its ability to
retain its original shape and size after the removal of the deforming force, undergoing plastic
deformation instead. It represents the maximum load a body can withstand without
undergoing plastic deformation. As a safety measure, it is common practice to prescribe only
one-third of the elastic limit's weight to ensure proper elasticity and avoid permanent
deformation of the material.
