  Some Terms

Stress – strain curve:
The stress strain curve has been shown in the fig.




Fig 8.16: Stress- Strain curve


From the point of origin to point A, stress is proportional to the strain, following
Hooke’s law, and hence this point is called the proportional limit point. From point A
to B, a large strain is observed; however, the body remains within the elastic limit.
Upon applying stress beyond point B to point C, the wire does not return to its
original state, resulting in a permanent set. The material exhibits a dual nature of
elasticity and plasticity between these two points, and point C is therefore called the
yield point. Moving from point C to point D, there is a large strain, and point D is
known as the breaking stress point. Beyond point D, even a small stress causes
continuous stretching until the material breaks.

Ductile and Brittle Substance:
Substances that undergo continuous elongation until they break, experiencing plastic
deformation, are called ductile substances. Metals are prime examples of ductile
substances.
On the other hand, substances that break after surpassing the elastic limit are called
brittle substances. Glass is a well-known example of a brittle substance.


      The plastic region between the elastic limit (point B) and the fracture point (point E)
      determines the ductile nature of materials. A longer plastic region indicates greater
      ductility, while a shorter region signifies brittleness. Ductile materials, such as those
      used for bending wires, are preferred.
      Materials that do not follow Hooke’s law even within the elastic limit are called
      elastomers. Rubber is a prime example of this type.
A Few Terms:
      The elasticity of a body refers to its tendency to regain its original configuration after
      the removal of a deforming force. While some bodies immediately regain their
      configuration, others may take some time. This delay in regaining the original
      configuration is called the elastic after-effect.
      For materials like quartz and phosphor bronze, the elastic after-effect is negligible,
      whereas for materials like glass fiber, it is significant. This difference explains why
      suspension coils in moving coil galvanometers are made of quartz and phosphor bronze.
   1. Elastic after-effect for a perfectly elastic body is zero.
   2. Elastic after-effect for a perfectly inelastic body is infinite.

Elastic Hysteresis

When a material wire is stretched several times to its original length using a deforming force,
the stress applied may not be proportional to the strain produced. However, the material regains
its original configuration through a different path after the removal of the deforming force.

Hence, the phenomenon of following different paths of increasing and decreasing stress is
called hysteresis. The loop formed in these two cases is known as the hysteresis loop.




Fig 8.17: Elastic Hysteresis


A high amount of work is required to stretch the wire compared to contracting it, leading to
the presence of a non-conservative force. The difference in the work done represents the
energy loss, which is balanced by the area of the hysteresis loop.
This phenomenon is the reason for using rubber as a vibration absorber, as rubber exhibits a
large hysteresis loop.

Elastic Fatigue
When a material is subjected to an alternating deforming force, it undergoes elongation and
contraction accordingly. After several cycles of elongation and contraction, the strain of the
material becomes large compared to the applied stress. Consequently, the material becomes


less elastic, leading to elastic fatigue or fatigue failure, similar to human beings experiencing
fatigue due to repeated exertion.
The effects of elastic fatigue are:
     3. Within the elastic limit, a wire can be broken.
     4. Without the use of equipment, a wire can be sliced into pieces.
     5. After a long period of service, railway tracks and bridges are deemed unsafe.
     6. After a long period of usage, spring balances give incorrect readings.

text:
Heat and temperature

                                        Anders Celsius (27 November 1701 – 25 April 1744) was
                                        a Swedish astronomer, physicist and mathematician. He was
                                        professor of astronomy at Uppsala University from 1730 to
                                        1744, but traveled from 1732 to 1735 visiting notable
                                        observatories in Germany, Italy and France. He founded
                                        the Uppsala Astronomical Observatory in 1741, and in 1742
                                        proposed (an inverted form of) the Centigrade temperature scale
 Anders Celsius (1701-1744)             which was later renamed Celsius in his honour.

Think?
    1. What do we feel cold or warm, when we pick
 Andersup
       Celsius (1701-1744)
          ice blocks in our hands?
    2. Do you have any idea why it happens?
    3. What do we feel cold or hot if we accidentally
       touch the laundry iron base during plug-in?
    4. Do you have any idea why it happens?



                                                                         [Fig. 9.1]




                      [Fig.9.2]


9.1 Introduction
Heat and temperature have a great influence on the behavior of matter and the world around
us. They have a fundamental role in all events from the everyday experience of feeling warmth
from the sun to the complex processes of thermal equilibrium and heat transfer in various
systems. Heat and temperature are closely related. Heat refers to the transfer of thermal energy
between systems as a result of temperature difference whereas temperature is a measure of the
average kinetic energy of molecules within a system. Thermal energy is the result of molecular


randomness (kinetic energy) within a system. In this chapter, we study the definitions,
properties, and applications of thermal energy, heat, and temperature to dig out their mysteries.

9.2 Thermal Energy
Thermal energy is the most basic form of energy contained within a system or an atom. Thermal
energy is not in transit but remains stored in the system as its kinetic energy. Thermal energy
is responsible for random movements of the molecules, or atoms, and that makes the atoms and
molecules move faster. Thermal energy gives the total kinetic energy possessed by a system.
Therefore, the thermal energy of a body is responsible for its temperature. In a system, it
increases with an increase in temperature and hence it is used to determine the internal energy
of such a system. Internal energy includes the kinetic energy and potential energy of molecules
within a substance. The kinetic energy component of internal energy is directly related to the
thermal energy of the system.
Thermal energy has been used for heating, boiling water and cooking food , etc. since the
beginning of the human race. From the beginning, the primary sources of the thermal energy
were the sun and fire, but technological evolution over the years has expanded the scope to
new man-made energy sources such as geothermal energy, nuclear heat, waste heat, and
electrical energy. Chemical energy and wind energy are other sources of thermal energy used
throughout.
Observations reveal that a hot object possesses a considerable amount of thermal energy, while
a cold object has a smaller amount. This concept can be illustrated by a common experience:
rubbing our hands together on a freezing winter day. In this scenario, the kinetic energy of our
hands is transformed into thermal energy through the friction generated between them.
When a substance is heated, its temperature increases because the average kinetic energy of the
molecules increases. At a higher temperature, molecules have greater kinetic energy and move
more rapidly. This increased motion leads to more frequent and energetic collisions between
molecules. Consequently, thermal energy is transferred from the higher temperature region to
the lower temperature. This transfer of thermal energy is known as heat.


9.3 Heat
When we place a hot object in thermal contact with a cold object, the thermal energy gets
transferred from the hot object into the cold one until they attain thermal equilibrium. This
thermal energy in transit is commonly referred to as heat. Hence, heat energy is the transfer of
thermal energy between two objects at different temperatures. Heat, being a form of energy, is
not a physical object; therefore, we cannot sense it by merely looking at an object, but rather
feel it when we touch it. The Sun stands out as a significant and natural source of heat energy.
In contemporary times, the heat energy, we primarily use is derived from natural sources like
gas and oil.
When we are exposed to sun light, we feel warm. Similarly, when we go near the snow covered
hill we feel cold. Also, if we touch the snow we feel further cold. In all cases energy is


exchanged with our body. In the former case, our body has gained some energy from sunlight
but in the later cases, our body has lost some energy. This exchange of energy is carried out by
the difference in hotness between our body and sunlight in the first case and between our body
and snow in the later cases. In all above cases, the exchanged amount of energy or energy in
transit is heat. Hence, heat is the energy which is transferred on the account of temperature
difference between one body and another body. The natural transfer of heat is a non-mechanical
process.
It is not necessary for the heat to flow from a body which has more heat energy to a body which
has less heat energy. For example; A full bucket of warm water contains more heat energy than
a red, hot iron nail. But if we immerse the nail in warm water heat will flow from the nail to
the warm water to attain thermal equilibrium.
In the molecular concept, all substances are composed of large number of molecules. These
molecules are in random motion except at the absolute zero temperature. Therefore, they
possess kinetic energy. “The sum of the kinetic energy of all molecules of a substance is the
measure of heat energy contained in that substance”.
Heat is the energy in transit or exchange amount of energy and can be measured by using
calorimeter. SI unit of heat is joule (J) but commonly heat is measured in calorie (cal). Such
that1 cal = 4.18 J.
Thermal energy is the energy contained in a system but heat is the flow of thermal energy.

Comparisons between thermal energy and heat
S.N.     Thermal energy                                 Heat

Cause    It is due to the movement of molecules or It is due to difference in the degree of
         atoms in a system.                        hotness or coldness of a system

Change It increases as the temperature of a system It always flows from the hot body towards
       increases due to an increase in the movement the cold body until both attain equal
       of particles.                                temperature.

                                                     It is the transfer of thermal energy.
         energy.

Source   Sources of thermal energy are geothermal Natural sources of heat are coal, gas, oil,
         energy, solar energy, friction, etc.     etc.

9.4 Temperature
Temperature is the degree of hotness or coldness of a body which determines the direction of
heat flow. When two bodies at different temperatures are brought in thermal contact then the
cold body warms up and the hot body cools down. Due to the difference in the thermal state
(hotness), heat is lost by hot body which is transferred towards cold body. Hence heat of cold
body increases. Thus, the temperature is the thermal state of a body which determines the
direction of heat flow between two bodies in thermal contact.
In thermal contact, the temperature of a cold body goes on increasing and the temperature of a
hot body goes on decreasing until both acquire the same value of temperature. Hence


temperature of a system is the property which finally acquires the same value as all other bodies
placed in the thermal contact.
The body which loses heat in thermal contact is said to be at higher temperature whereas the body
which gains heat is said to be at lower temperature. The body which gains heat goes on warming
up and its temperature increases due to added heat energy. Hence temperature is the effect of
heat.
A body at higher temperature gives more severe pain of hotness even if it may have low amount
of heat. But a body at low temperature gives less severe pain of hotness even if it may have
high amount of heat.
In molecular concept, temperature of a body gives the measure of average kinetic energy of its
molecules. It is not defined for single particle but for a system of large number of particles.
Hence temperature is macroscopic parameter.
The unit of temperature is Kelvin (K) in SI system and other commonly used units are degree
Celsius (C) and degree Fahrenheit (F).

9.5 Effects of Heat
When heat is applied to a body, it may bring the following changes:
1. Thermoelectric effect: If a temperature difference is maintained between two junctions of
   a closed loop made from a pair of dissimilar metal wires, an emf is developed. This emf
   produces electric current in the circuit. This effect of heat is called thermoelectric effect.
2. Generation of light energy: When we increase the temperature of a substance sufficiently
   high, the substance starts emitting light.
3. Change in electrical resistance: On increasing the temperature, electrical resistance of a
   conductor increases but in case of semiconductor electrical resistance decreases.
4. Change in physical properties: Change in temperature, volume, state, colour, viscosity,
   elasticity, solubility rate, rate of chemical reaction and surface tension, etc. are the physical
   changes carried out by the application of heat.
5. Change in chemical properties: Ignition of paper, boiling of egg, etc. are the examples of
   chemical changes carried out by the application of heat.
   Sample Questions:
   1. Can an object be hotter than another if they are at the same temperature? Explain.
   2. What is the temperature of a vacuum?
   3. Why does heat flow from a body at higher temperature to a body at lower temperature?
   4. Which factor determines the flow of heat between two bodies in thermal contact?


9.6 Thermal Equilibrium




                                 Fig. 9.3: Thermal Equilibrium


When a cup of hot tea is put on the table and after a short period of time, the temperature of the
tea will also be same as that of the surroundings. This is because when two bodies at different
temperatures are brought in thermal contact, heat flows from a body at higher temperature to a
body at lower temperature. So, temperature of hot body goes on decreasing and temperature of
cold body goes on increasing until both acquire equal value of temperature. After attaining equal
temperature net flow of heat between those bodies becomes zero, and they are said to be thermal
equilibrium. Actually, exchange of heat between two bodies in thermal contact does not stop at
thermal equilibrium, but it occurs at same rate in opposite direction. Using this idea of thermal
equilibrium temperature readings are taken otherwise a thermometer is worthless because it
always registers the temperature of its own thermometric substance.
“Two bodies are said to be in thermal equilibrium if there is no net flow of heat between them
even if they are in thermal contact”. In other words, two physical systems are in thermal
equilibrium if there is no net flow of thermal energy between them when they are in thermal
contact. Principle of thermal equilibrium is used to measure the temperature of a body from a
thermometer.

9.7 Thermal Equilibrium as a Working Principle of Mercury Thermometer
To measure the temperature of a body, the bulb of the thermometer and the object whose
temperature is to be measured are brought into thermal contact, and sufficient time is allowed
for them to reach thermal equilibrium. At thermal equilibrium, both the thermometric substance
and the object attain the same temperature. However, the temperature reading is solely
indicated by the thermometer, representing the temperature of its thermometric substance.
Therefore, the reading displayed by the thermometer is the temperature of its own thermometric
substance. By employing the concept of thermal equilibrium, we can infer that this temperature
is also the temperature of the given object. Thus, the principle of thermal equilibrium is
employed in measuring the temperature of a body using a thermometer.

9.8 Zeroth Law of Thermodynamics
Statement:“When two bodies A and B are in thermal equilibrium separately with a third body
C then, first two bodies A and B themselves must be in thermal equilibrium”.


                          C                                         C


                     A        B                                 A       B
                                       Diathermic wall



                                     Adiabatic wall
                         [Fig. 9.4, Zeroth law of thermodynamics]
Consider two bodies A and B which are separated by non-conducting wall. Let both are
separately connected with system C by conducting wall as shown in figure 9.4. If bodies are
kept in such contact for sometimes, then body A and B separately exchange their heat with
body C. Finally, both A and B separately attain thermal equilibrium with C. When adiabatic
wall between A and B is replaced by diathermic wall and they are separated from C by adiabatic
wall as in second figure, then A and B both exhibit no change in temperature. This indicates
that A and B were already in thermal equilibrium. This verifies the Zeroth law of
thermodynamics.


Long after the use of first and second law of thermodynamics Ralph Howard Fowler, in 1931,
formulated this law for the very fundamental single valued function (temperature). Hence this
law was labeled as Zeroth law of thermodynamics.

9.9 Thermometry




                                             [ Fig.9.5, A thermometer]
Thermometry is the science of temperature and its measurement and the device used to measure
the temperature is called thermometer. Working principle of thermometer is that the change in
temperature brings some changes in measurable physical properties of a body. For example;
change in,
 i. Length of bar                            ii.    Volume of liquid
iii. Volume of gas at constant pressure      iv.    Pressure of gas at constant volume
v. Magnetic properties of substance          vi.    Electrical resistance of a wire, etc.


To measure the temperature of a body, the bulb of thermometer and object whose temperature
is to be measured are brought in thermal contact and certain time is provided to bring them in
thermal equilibrium. The main three steps of thermometry are:
i. Construction
ii. Calibration
iii. Sensitiveness


                              [ Fig.9.6, Calibration of a thermometer]


Construction: A thermometer is constructed in such a way that the uniform variation in
properties of thermometric substance with temperature is maintained. Thermometric
substances may be solid, liquid or gas, and must be highly sensitive toward temperature change.
Calibration: While calibrating a thermometer, at first two standard degree of hotness (fixed
points) are noted and then units are provided by dividing the interval between fixed points into
different number of equal parts. The numbers of equal parts are different in different
temperature scales.

Sensitiveness
As far as possible thermometer should be more sensitive so that;
  1. It can read the temperature of body immediately.
  2. It does not exchange large amount of heat with the body whose temperature is to be
       measured. It gives almost accurate reading.
  3. It can read even a very small change in temperature.

Upper fixed point (UFP): It is the temperature at which pure water boils under standard
atmospheric pressure.

Lower fixed point (LFP):It is the temperature at which pure ice melts under standard
atmospheric pressure.

9.10 Absolute Scale and Absolute Zero Temperature:
Temperatures expressed in Kelvin scale are absolute temperatures. The zero value of
temperature in this scale is called absolute zero temperature. Absolute zero temperature is the
lowest possible temperature which can exist in the universe. Temperature which is 273
divisions below the lower fixed point of Kelvin scale, and has value of –273.15°C is absolute
zero temperature. At this temperature molecular motion stops and total kinetic energy of
molecules becomes zero. It is highly condensed state of matter.


Importance of Absolute Zero Temperature: Temperature of a body is directly proportional
to the kinetic energy of its molecules. Absolute temperature becomes zero only for the zero
kinetic energy of molecules. For zero kinetic energy, velocity of all molecules must be zero.
This means at absolute zero temperature molecules of a body are completely at rest.

Thermal Expansion
William Thomson, also known as Lord Kelvin, was one of the most
eminent scientists (a British physicist and mathematician) of the
nineteenth century, and is best known today for inventing the
international system of absolute temperature that bears his name.
Thomson held a position as Professor of Natural Philosophy at the
University of Glasgow.
Kelvin’s main achievements include the establishment of an
absolute heat scale, publishing some studies on the systems of
measurement units and patenting measuring devices such as the
galvanometer, helping to perfect transmissions through submarine
cables. He led to the establishment of absolute zero. Thomson also
became the first scientist to serve in the House of Lords.

10.1 Introduction
Thermal expansion is a fundamental concept in physics, which describes the change in size of
a substance under the application of heat. When the temperature of a material increases under
the application of heat, the atoms or molecules within the material begin to vibrate more,
causing the average distance between them to increase. This results in the expansion of the
material’s length, area and volume.
Thermal expansion is a phenomenon that affects a wide range of materials from solid s and
liquids to gases. The degree of thermal expansion varies depending on the material’s


composition, molecular structure, and the strength of intermolecular forces. The water exhibits
the unique behavior that it contracts as the temperature increases from 0C to 4C before
expanding upon further heating.
The knowledge of thermal expansion is very crucial in the fields of engineering, architecture
material science, etc. It plays a significant role in the designing and construction of structures,
the development of precision instruments, and the study of thermal behavior of the materials.
This chapter will explore the principles of thermal expansion, different types of thermal
expansion, and their applications in various contexts.

10.2 Thermal expansion
In the first demonstration, the size of the ball has been changed due to the application of heat.
Also, in the second demonstration, the size of the vessel as well as that of the liquid has been
changed due to the application of heat. These two demonstrations prove that when heat is given
to a body, not only its temperature rises but its size also increases.
When heat is applied to a body, the kinetic energy of its molecules increases. An increase in
kinetic energy causes an increase in the amplitude of molecular vibration as well as an increase
in molecular velocity. That is molecules move far apart giving greater intermolecular gap. As
a result, the size of the body increases and it occupies more space than before. This increase
in the size of a body due to the application of heat is called thermal expansion.

10.3 Linear Expansion

expansion can be observed by measuring the change in diameter of a circular plate or the
change in length of a rod or wire, etc.

10.8 Force Set-Up Due to Expansion or Contraction and Thermal Stress
If a metal bar is heated it will expand, but if we prevent it from
expanding then large forces will be set up within the bar. The force
will be that which would be needed to compress the bar to its
                                                                              F            F
original length from the expanded position. This force is called
force set up due to expansion. Similarly, if a metallic wire tied
between two rigid poles is cooled, it will try to contract but will
not be able to do so because of rigid poles. Instead, a large force
is set up to prevent the phenomenon of contraction. This force is [Fig;10.10 Force set up due to expansion]
called force set up due to contraction.
The mechanical force that occurs in an object when it is prevented either from expansion
during heating or from contraction during cooling is called force set-up due to expansion
or contraction.
Mathematically, it is given by F = YA   ; where Y= Young’s Modulus of elasticity, A=
cross-sectional area,  = thermal strain.
The stress corresponding to this force is called Thermal stress.

The bimetallic thermostat is a device made up of two thin metallic strips of different linear
expansivities welded together along their lengths. Brass - steel bimetallic strips are the
examples of bimetallic thermostat. When brass-steel thermostat is heated, the brass having
greater value of linear expansivity expands more than the steel. Since the two strips are welded
together, the thermostat bends into an arc with brass in greater curvature. As a result, electric
contact breaks as in figure 10.11(b). This special design can be used as safety measure to
control the overflow of heat in many electrical appliances, and hence to save from accidents.

       Henri Victor Regnault was a French chemist and physicist
         best known for his careful measurements of the thermal

        and was a mentor to William Thomson in the late 1840s.
       Regnault designed an apparatus for a large number

       He showed that no two gases have precisely the same

11.1    Introduction
If two bodies are brought in thermal contact then the hotter body cools down and the colder
body warms up until they attain equilibrium temperature. During this process, energy is
transferred from the hotter body to the colder body. This energy in transit is called heat. The
transfer of heat continues whenever the temperature difference exists between two bodies.
Therefore, heat is a form of energy and is a scalar quantity. We cannot directly measure the
quantity of heat on the body; instead, it can be measured as the quantity of heat transferred
from one body to another.
The quantity of heat transferred in a process may change the temperature of the body. For a
given value of heat exchange, the change in temperature will depend upon the mass of the body
and the nature of the material of the body. By knowing the value of the temperature change,
mass and specific heat capacity (nature of substance), we can calculate the quantity of heat
exchanged by a body. When the thermos flask, which contains a liquid is shaken vigorously,
the temperature of the liquid gets raised without supplying heat. A similar phenomenon can be
observed in the case of gases. In both cases, work done on the system becomes a source of heat
energy.


Calorimetry
We can measure the quantity of heat transfer from one body to another body. The science of
measurement of the transfer of heat is calorimetry. Thus, calorimetry is a branch of physics
which deals with the experimental techniques for the quantitative measurement of heat
exchange. A device used for the measurement of heat transfer is called a calorimeter.

A calorimeter is a device used for the quantitative measurement of heat exchange. Generally,
calorimeters are made up of copper because copper has low specific heat capacity and its
specific heat capacity is almost constant for all temperature ranges.
A calorimeter is a thin-walled, and polished cylindrical metallic vessel generally made of
copper as shown in fig. 11.1. It consists of a stirrer of the same material. The calorimeter is
well insulated so that the exchange of heat between the system and surroundings gets
prohibited. To provide insulation, the calorimeter is wrapped in wool, cotton, or any other
insulating materials and kept inside a wooden box. For the measurement of the temperature of
the calorimeter and its contents, a thermometer is inserted through a hole made in the sliding
lid of the wooden box.

11.2 Heat Equation
When we heat a body, it absorbs heat and gets hotter until it stays in the same state. Likewise,
when a body cools down, it loses heat, and its temperature drops until it stays in the same state.
The heat equation is a mathematical relationship between heat absorbed or released by a body
with its mass, specific heat capacity and change in temperature.
Experimentally, it is found that the amount of heat energy absorbed or released by a body is,
i. directly proportional to the mass of the body (m),

ii. directly proportional to the change in temperature of the body (),

Here, s is known as the specific heat capacity of the material of the body.
Equation (3) is known as heat equation.
 One calorie: 1 calorie is defined as the amount of heat needed to raise the temperature of 1
 gram of pure water by 1 degree Celsius (generally from 14.5C to 15.5C). 1 cal = 4.2 J


11.3 Heat Capacity or Thermal Capacity
Heat capacity or thermal capacity of a body is defined as the amount of heat required to change
the temperature of given mass of the body through 1°C (or 1 K).
If Q is the amount of heat required to change the temperature of a body of mass m through
then
       Q = m s                [s is specific heat capacity of the body]
If the temperature changes by unit value i.e. = 1°C then,
       Q = ms
This quantity of heat is called heat capacity of given body. Hence, heat capacity is the
product of mass and specific heat capacity of the body. Heat capacity depends on nature
and mass of the body. The heat capacity is measured in JK -1 .

This indicates that the change in the temperature of a substance is inversely

11.6 Applications of High and Low Specific Heat Capacity
A substance which has value of specific heat capacity can absorb large amount of heat from
any object brought in thermal contact. As a result of this, temperature of object in contact
reduces by sufficiently large value but its own temperature changes almost negligibly. This
property of substance can be used as cooling agent. Water has high specific heat capacity and
shows such behavior. Therefore, water can be used,
      (i)      as cooling agent in many heating appliances and in running vehicles
      (ii)     to lower down temperature of a person suffering from high fever.
Also, a substance which has high value of specific heat capacity can release large amount of
heat to anybody brought in thermal contact. As a result of this, temperature of object in contact
increases by sufficiently large value but its own temperature changes almost negligibly. This
property of substance can be used as heating agent. Water has high specific heat capacity and
shows such behavior. Therefore, water can be used
      (i)      as heating agent in room heating system
      (ii)     as heating agent in hot water bag


Substance which has low value of specific heat capacity can absorb or lose almost negligible
amount of heat from or to any other body brought in thermal contact and immediately it attains
thermal equilibrium. This action does not bring any change in thermal configuration of the
body in contact. Mercury has such property. Therefore, mercury can be used as thermometric
substance.
Similarly copper also has low value of specific heat capacity so that it can be used as material
of calorimeter.
Also, substance which has low value of specific heat capacity suffers sufficiently large change
in temperature even from the small amount of heat applied. Cooking oil has such property.
Therefore, cooking oil can be used to make fried food items (easier and faster cooking).
Similarly massage oil has low specific heat capacity so that it gets heated sufficiently from the
heat of friction during massage.

11.7 Newton's Law of Cooling

Have you ever held a warm bowl full of food in your hand, and wondered why it seems to cool
down rapidly at first but stays lukewarm for much longer? Also, the hot soup will be too hot
to eat for the first few minutes, but eventually, it reaches a temperature we can enjoy it. Then
we can eat the soup leisurely over some more minutes, and it stays warm for much longer. We
may have a query that how fast a cup of boiling water will cool down in a kitchen at room
temperature. In all of above activities, there is a relationship between temperature difference
of hot substance with its surroundings and the time taken by it to cool down. Newton's law of
cooling describes how fast a substance cools down. Also, it establishes a relationship between
the temperature of a substance and the time taken by the substance to cool down.

During cooling of hot liquid exposed to the surroundings of lower temperature, liquid loses
heat continuously to the surroundings until it attains the equilibrium. The amount of heat lost
by the liquid depends on different factors like nature of liquid, nature of solid vessel, surface
area of liquid exposed to the surroundings, temperature difference of liquid and its
surroundings, etc. The loss of heat by different processes may be explained by different laws.
If the temperature difference is maintained suitable (less than 35C) and all other factors which
affect the amount of heat lost are made constant then, cooling of liquid follows the Newton’s
law of cooling.

11.8 Principle of Calorimetry
Can you answer this?
A student claims that when two bodies at different temperatures are brought in thermal contact,
fall in temperature of hotter body must be equal to the rise in temperature of the colder one. Is
it acceptable?
When two objects at different temperatures are brought into thermal contact, the hotter object
loses the heat while the colder object gains the heat until both reach to an equal temperature. If
heat loss to the surroundings is prevented, the quantity of heat lost by the hotter body is equal
to the quantity of heat gained by the colder body. This is the principle of calorimetry. It can be
stated that the amount of the heat lost by a hotter body must be equal to amount of the heat
gained by a colder body during the process of heat exchange between two objects in a closed
system.
That is, heat loss= heat gain ; for a closed system.
A closed system is also called an isolated system. In a closed system objects under
consideration do not exchange heat with its surroundings. Principle of calorimetry is an
alternative form of the law of conservation of energy. Idea of principle of calorimetry is used
to calculate specific heat capacity of different substances.


11.9 Determination of Specific Heat Capacity of a Solid by the Method of Mixture
Regnault's apparatus can be used to determine the specific heat capacity of a substance by the
method of mixture. In the method of mixture, we use principle of calorimetry to calculate
specific heat capacity.
Procedure

11.10 Change of Phase
Do you know?
   Even if you add heat to an object, the temperature of the object may not change.
Matters exist in three different states. Therefore, substances found around us may fall under
either of these three states: solid, liquid, and gas. A solid state has the least intermolecular
space, the liquid state has a moderate value of intermolecular space, and the gaseous state has
sufficient large intermolecular space. The state of a substance is the result of heat applied, or
the pressure exerted, or both to the object. Common changes of the state include melting,
freezing, sublimation, deposition, condensation, and vaporization. A change of a state is a
physical change in a matter.

continuous cooling of the liquid state reduces the temperature of an object continuously to a

is supplied or it is dragged out to change the state of a matter. Fusion and solidification,
vaporization and condensation, sublimation and deposition are pairs of reverse processes of
change of phase.
The amount of heat required to convert the state of matter at a constant temperature is called the


latent heat of the matter. The latent heat during the change of state from solid to liquid or vice-
versa is called the latent heat of fusion. The latent heat during the change of state from liquid to
gas or vice-versa is called the latent heat of vaporization. Latent heat is called so because it is
hidden from the thermometer reading. Latent heat is also called heat of transformation.
During the change of state of a matter, heat is used for two purposes; one to overcome the external
atmospheric pressure to create a space for expansion, and the next to reduce the intermolecular
force of attraction. The former is called external latent heat and latter is called internal latent heat.
External latent heat is much smaller than internal latent heat. Value of both types of heat are
much greater in case of conversion of state from liquid to gas than that in the case of conversion
of state from solid to liquid. Therefore, the latent heat of vaporization is always greater than the
latent heat of fusion.
Latent heat cannot be measured in terms of change in velocity and change in kinetic energy of
molecules. But, energy can neither be created nor can it be destroyed. Hence, during the change
of phase, heat is used to increase potential energy molecules but not kinetic energy. Therefore,
heat can also be considered as potential energy.

11.14 Boiling
A fast and noisy process of conversion of liquid into vapour at a constant temperature is called
boiling. During boiling, liquid takes certain amount of heat as latent heat. The temperature at
which liquid changes into vapour (gas) is called the boiling point. Different objects have different
values of boiling point. Boiling point of water is 100 o C at 760mm of Hg pressure.


Effect of Pressure on Boiling Point
Even for a single object, the boiling point varies according to the pressure exerted on it. The
actual boiling point of a liquid is the temperature at which the saturated vapor pressure of the
liquid becomes equal to the external (atmospheric) pressure on its surface. The boiling point of
a liquid increases with an increase in pressure, and decreases with a decrease in pressure.
Further, pressure decreases with an increase in altitude, and increases with a decrease in
altitude. Therefore, the boiling point is a function of pressure, which, in turn, is a function of
altitude. For example, water boils at a lower temperature in Solukhumbu than in Birgunj, and
rice is cooked faster in a pressure cooker than in an open pot.

11.15 Evaporation
We feel cold when we spray perfume on our body. Similarly, we experience a cooling sensation
in our mouth when we eat Halls. Can you explain the physics behind these phenomena? Both
cases involve the cooling effect of evaporation.
A slow and silent process of conversion of liquid into vapour at all temperature below its
boiling point is called evaporation. Evaporation takes place from the surface of a liquid.
During evaporation, molecules escape from the surface of a liquid, and convert into vapour.
Those molecules take necessary latent heat of conversion from the neighboring molecules and
hence the temperature of the remaining mass of liquid decreases. This effect is called cooling
effect of evaporation.

Some examples of Evaporation
   a. After sweating, we feel cool due to the evaporation of the sweat from our body’s heat.
   b. Washed or wet clothes are dried by evaporation. When the clothes are hung outside in
      the sun, due to the heat of the sun, the water droplets present in the clothes get dried
      away due to evaporation.
   c. Spirits are also compounds that evaporate at a very low temperature. Hence it is used
      to sterilize the skin where a syringe for vaccines or blood collection needs to be
      introduced.
   d. Evaporation occurs in the water cycle in which the water from any water body on the
      surface of the earth is evaporated into the air. This water when cools down causes rain.
   e. A person feels cold only while coming out in open air after having a bath in the bathroom
      but not inside the bathroom.

11.16 Effect of Pressure on Melting Point of Substance
    Do you Know?
 i.   An avalanche originates when a large amount of snow collects at a location.
ii.   A large iceberg melts at the base but not at the top.
    Same physics is behind these two phenomena. In both activities, main role is of pressure.
    Melting point of solid is greatly affected by pressure applied on it. The effect of pressure on
    melting point is different for different substances.
    For the substances like cast iron and ice whose volume decreases while melting, their


   melting point decreases with increase in pressure.
   For the substances like wax and lead whose volume increases while melting, their melting
   point increases with increase in pressure.

When two pieces of ice are pressed against each other, pressure on the contact portion increases
and hence melting point decreases to that portion. As a result, ice melts in contact portion. If
applied pressure is removed again, the melting point increases to initial value. Now water, so
formed after melting of ice, freezes. During this process two pieces of ice join to form a single
piece. Hence, when pressure is applied to ice, it melts and as soon as the pressure is removed,
it freezes again. We refer to this phenomenon as regelation. Regelation is the phenomenon of
melting of ice under the application of pressure/compression and its freezing after the removal
of applied pressure.

A graph between pressure and temperature which has three curves; namely fusion curve,
vaporization curve and sublimation curve is called phase diagram. It is also called P-T diagram.


The phase diagram clearly explains the three different phases of a matter. The phase diagram
of water is shown in figure 11.8.
    a. Vaporization curve (steam line): The graph showing variation of boiling point
       of a substance with the pressure is called vaporization curve. The substance
       exists in liquid state above the steam line and it exists in gaseous state below
       steam line.
    b. Fusion curve (Ice line): The graph showing the variation of the melting point of
       substance with pressure is called fusion curve. A substance exists in solid state
       above the ice line and it exists in liquid state below ice line.
    c. Sublimation curve (Hoar-frost line): The graph showing the variation of sublimation
       point of substance with pressure is called sublimation curve or hoar-frost line. At very
       low temperature and pressure, substances are found to sublimate. For example, solid
       carbon dioxide (dry ice) sublimates even at atmospheric pressure. A substance exists
       in solid state above the hoar-frost line and it exists in gaseous state below hoar-
       frost line.


Triple Point
Triple point of a substance is the point in P-T diagram representing a particular value of
temperature and pressure at which all three states of that substance can co-exist.
Triple point of a substance can also be defined as the point in phase diagram at which
vaporization curve, fusion curve and sublimation curve of given substance intersect each other.
The triple point of water is (0.006 atm., 0.01°C) and that of carbon dioxide is (5.11 atm., –
56.6°C)

Rate of Heat Flow

Josef Stefan was born to Slovenian parents in St. Peter, Austria,
and he graduated from the university of Vienna in 1857. At the
University of Vienna, he rose from lecturer in mathematical
physicist in 1858 to professor Ordinarius of physics in 1863 and to
the director of the Physical Institute in 1866. Five years after he
derived his law of black body radiation empirically, it was derived
theoretically by Ludwig Boltzmann of Austria, and hence became
known as the Stefan-Boltzmann law.
Stefan- Boltzmann law states that the radiant energy of a black
body (a theoretical object that absorbs all radiation that falls on it)
is proportional to the fourth power of its absolute temperature. This
law was one of the first important steps toward the understanding
of the black body which gave the base for the quantum idea of
                                                                          Josef Stefan (1835-1893)
radiation.                                                                (1835-1893)

     2. Tanks of gasoline are generally painted with aluminum paints.
     3. The earth constantly receives heat radiations from the sun and gets warmed up.

We have many examples in our periphery where heat is

There are three different methods of transfer of heat. For example; when one end of a metallic
rod is heated, the other end also gets heated. When a liquid in a vessel is heated from the
bottom, the upper surface of the liquid also gets heated. We receive the heat from a very hot
object, and from the sun directly.
Transfer of heat due to molecular vibrations in a solid as in the case of a metallic rod is called
conduction. Transfer of heat due to actual molecular translation in fluid is called convection.
Boiling of water is an example of convection. Transfer of heat without the support of any
material medium is called radiation e.g., receiving heat from the sun.

12.2    Conduction

When one end of a solid is heated, atoms in this hotter region vibrate with greater amplitude
and have more kinetic energy than the neighboring atoms in the colder region. The atoms in
the hotter region collide with the neighboring atoms in the colder region. During the process,
hotter molecules give up some energy to colder molecules. The same phenomena occur
between each set of neighboring atoms and the process continues up to the next end. This
method of heat transfer is called conduction. Conduction also takes place between two different
bodies if they are in thermal contact.
Therefore, conduction is defined as the process of transfer of heat from one point to
another point of a body, carried out by means of collisions between rapidly vibrating
atoms in the hotter region and slowly vibrating atoms in the colder region. There is no


actual transfer of particles during conduction.
Material medium is required for the conduction. Molecular collisions enhanced by molecular
vibrations are the means of conduction of heat.
The ability of anybody to conduct heat is measured in terms of thermal conductivity.
Generally, metals have a high value of thermal conductivity. Therefore, metals are called good
conductors of heat. The materials which do not conduct heat are called bad conductors. For
example; paper, air, plastic, wood, etc.

Examples and Applications of Thermal Conduction in Our Daily Life
1. Two thin jackets are warmer than a single jacket of the same thickness because the air
    particles trapped between two jackets minimize the conduction.
2. The Eskimo houses are double-walled so that the air trapped between two walls behaves as
    a bad conductor, and prevents the flow of heat from inside to outside.
3. In cold countries, windows have two panes of glass with a thin layer of air in between.
4. Thick walls are constructed in cold storage rooms.
5. To remove a stopper fitted tightly to the bottle, the neck is immersed in warm water and gently
    heated. The glass neck being a bad conductor expands but does not conduct heat to the
    stopper. So that the stopper can be removed easily.
6. Sauce pans, hot water buckets, kettles, etc. are made of metal but their handles are of wooden
    or ebonite or Bakelite so that heat from utensils cannot conduct to hand.
7. Woolen clothes have fine pores filled with air. Air and wool both are bad conductors of heat.
    So that the flow of heat from the body to outside the atmosphere is prevented. Therefore,
    woolen clothes provide good insulation and keep our body warm in winter.
8. In a thermos bottle, a vacuum is created between two surfaces to avoid the transfer of heat
    due to conduction.
9. We feel iron chairs colder than wooden chairs in winter.
10. Ice is packed in saw-dust inside double-walled ice box wrapped in gunny bags to prevent
    from melting.
11. Quilts are filled with fluffy cotton. Cotton can trap air in its pores. Both cotton and air are
    bad conductors and provide good insulation. As a result, the flow of heat is prevented, and
    keeps our body warm. A newly built quilt can trap more air as it contains more pores than
    an old one. Therefore, a newly built quilt is warmer than an old one.

12.6 Convection

Convection is the process of transfer of heat in fluids by means of the actual motion of heated
particles from high temperature region to low temperature region. Heating of water, land


breezes, sea breezes, winds, etc. are some examples of convection. In convection, heated
particles carry heat and move from the hotter region to the colder region, but the cold particles
move in opposite directions. Convection is possible only in liquid and gas but not in solid and
vacuum. There are two types of convection; natural convection and artificial convection.




[Fig;12.6 convection; forced convection and natural convection]


Natural or Free Convection;
Natural convection is also called free convection. The primary circulation of the Earth's
atmosphere causing daily weather results, land breezes, sea breezes, and trade winds are
examples of natural convection. Natural convection is the most commonly brought about by
local change in density which is ultimately associated with pressure difference or temperature
difference between two regions of fluid. Buoyant force is responsible for movement of particles
during natural convection, and it is impossible in gravity-free region.


Artificial or Forced Convection;
If convection is carried out by maintaining pressure difference mechanically by a pump or a
blower or by any means of external aid then the convection is called artificial convection or forced
convection. Pumping up the blood by the heart and its circulation through the different parts is an
example of forced convection. This process keeps our body warm. Also, the use of fans to cool
an electronic equipment using water heaters or geysers for instant heating of water are
examples of forced convection.

Examples of Convection:
   a) Trade winds
    Winds are due to convection current set up in the atmosphere by uneven heating in different
   locations. The Earth's surface gets heated more at the equator than at the poles. Therefore,
   warm air rises from the equator. To fill up the vacant space, the cold air from the poles
   moves towards the equator. These motions of air are known as trade winds because these
   winds were used by ancient traders for sailing their vessels. Due to the west-to-east motion
   of the Earth, trade wind seems coming from the northeast in the northern hemisphere but it
   seems coming from the southwest in the southern hemisphere.
 b) Sea breezes and land breezes:




[Fig. 12.7, Land breeze and sea breeze]
      EXAMPLE 1                               Water has a large specific heat capacity. Because
   of this, during day time, seawater gets heated up slowly, and becomes less warm than the
   land surface near the sea. Therefore, the air molecules in contact with land become
   comparatively hotterand lighter. The lighter air molecules move upward. The vacant space
   above the land surface is filled by the comparatively cold and heavier air molecules coming
   from the sea surface. As a result, a large mass of air moves towards the sea-shore from sea.
   This is called sea breeze. During nighttime, a similar process takes place but in the opposite
   direction, and air mass moves towards the sea surface from the sea-shore. The process is
   called land breeze.
c) Ocean Currents:
   In the ocean which extends from the pole even up to the equator, water gets heated more at
   the equator than at the poles. The water level rises at the equator due to a decrease in density.
   This water flows towards the poles. A current of water is set up which is known as hot
   current or gulfstream. At the mean time, the cold water moves to the opposite direction
   beneath the surface which is called undercurrent.
d) Ventilation:
Ventilators are provided near the ceiling of the rooms so that moisturized warm air and carbon
   dioxide in the upper layer go out through them. As a result, fresh air comes inside


   continuously from the windows and the doors.
e) Chimney:
   A chimney is provided above the fire in a room or kitchen so that continuous circulation of
   oxygen for combustion of fuel is possible.
f) Monsoons:
Monsoons are based on the principle of convection.
Sample Questions:
 1. Why is it hotter above the fire than by its side?
 2. If air is a bad conductor of heat, why do people not feel warm without clothes?
 3. Ventilations are provided near the ceilings in a room. Explain this statement.

12.7    Radiation

The heating of the Earth by the Sun and the transmission of heat around the fire are examples
of transfer of heat by radiation. The heating of a room with an open-hearth fireplace is another
example. The heat radiated by the flames, coals, and hot bricks are examples of transfer of heat
by radiation. The radiation takes place even in a vacuum. Radiation does not heat the medium
through which heat passes. Hence the radiation is the process of transmission of heat from one
point to another without need of any material medium. During radiation, heat is transferred in
the form electromagnetic wave and travel with speed of 3108 ms-1 in vacuum. Heat energy
radiated by an object is called radiant energy or thermal radiation. Radiation stands for heat
energy as well as for the process of transfer of heat.
Thermal Radiation
All objects can radiate energy continuously in the form of electromagnetic radiations at all
temperature above zero kelvin. This form of energy by virtue of temperature is called thermal
radiation. Thermal radiation exhibits the phenomena like reflection, refraction, interference,
polarization and diffraction. Wavelength and energy of thermal radiation depend upon
temperature and nature of the radiating body. Thermal radiation belongs to infrared region of
electromagnetic spectrum.
Examples of Transfer of Heat by Radiation
a. Reflectors of electric heaters are polished so that they reflect maximum heat to the room.
b. White clothes are preferred in summer but black clothes are preferred in winter.
   Radiations get reflected back from white clothes and this support us from overheating during
   summer. But radiations are absorbed by black clothes so that it keeps us warm during winter.
c. Hot water pipes and radiators used in rooms.
   These pipes are painted black inside the room so that they radiate maximum heat to the
   room, but they are painted white outside the room to prevent the loss of heat to the
   surroundings.
d. The junction of the thermocouple is painted black so that it can absorb maximum heat.

12.9   Black Body and Black Body Radiation

A perfectly black body is an idealized physical body that absorbs all incidents of heat radiation,
regardless of wavelengths or angle of incidence. Also, a perfectly black body emits radiations
of all possible wavelengths when heated. For a perfect black body, the value of absorptance is
unity, and that of emissivity is also unity. A good absorber is a good emitter. The sun emits
radiations of all wavelengths. So, it can be considered as a black body. A black body is a good
emitter so that it can emit radiation of all possible wavelengths. A perfectly black body cannot
absorb all the radiant energy but neither it reflects nor it transmits. Hence a perfect body appears
black at room temperature and is known as a black body. However, at higher temperatures, it
can actually glow at visible wavelengths. Therefore, the term 'black body' is also referred to an
object that glows. For example; the sun.
Black body radiation is given off not only by extremely hot objects but also by anything which
is above the absolute zero temperature. From stars to ice cubes, they may give black body
radiation.
A perfectly black body cannot be realized in actual practice. The nearest approach to a perfect
black body is a surface coated with lamp black or platinum black. Such a surface absorbs 96%
to 98% of the incident radiation. Ferry's black body is an example of perfect black body realized
in practice.

Ideal Gas

  Robert Boyle was an Anglo-Irish natural philosopher,
  chemist, physicist, and inventor. He was one of
  the most prolific figures in the scientific revolution and
  is often considered the first modern chemist, making
  him one of the founding fathers of modern chemistry
  and a pioneer of contemporary experimental scientific
  techniques.
  Boyle gave a very popular law which defines the
  inversely proportional connection between absolute
  pressure, and the volume of a gas in a closed system
  under constant temperature. Boyle was a polymath
  with diverse interests ranging from animal husbandry
  to underwater respiration, and from the study of
  ancient languages to finding ways of extending the
  human lifespan. Furthermore, Boyle had both the
  intellect and the financial resources to pursue such a
  wide research agenda.                                           Robert Boyle (1627-1691)
                                                                  (1627-1691)



Do you know?
   A kilogram of hydrogen has more atoms than a kilogram of iron.

13.1 Introduction
All the states of matter; solid, liquid and gas, do not exhibit the same behavior on the
application of heat. The applied heat cannot bring a significant change in pressure in the case
of solid and liquid. But in the case of gas, applied heat brings out the change in temperature,
volume as well as pressure. The properties, which the matter exhibits on the application of heat,
are called thermal properties. Velocity, kinetic energy, mass, etc. are microscopic properties
whereas pressure, temperature, volume, etc. are the macroscopic properties. Charles’ law,
Boyle’s Law, Dalton’s law, etc. are the interrelationships among the values of thermal
properties. By combining these laws in a special condition, the ideal gas equation can also be
derived. The ideal gas equation describes the thermodynamic state of a matter at its equilibrium.
The kinetic molecular theory of a gas assumes that the gas molecules exchange energy and
momentum during collisions with the wall of the container, and hence give pressure to the wall.
This theory explains about macroscopic properties of gas.

13.3 Absolute Zero Temperature
Temperature expressed in the Kelvin scale is known as absolute temperature. The zero value
of the absolute scale is called absolute zero temperature. At this temperature, the molecular
motion stops, and the kinetic energy becomes zero. Also, the absolute temperature is directly
proportional to the kinetic energy of its molecules and kinetic energy will never be negative. It
means, the absolute temperature cannot be negative. Therefore, absolute zero temperature is
the lowest possible temperature in the thermodynamic temperature scale. Hence, in other
words, absolute zero temperature is defined as the lowest possible temperature that can exist in
the universe. Till the date, the absolute zero temperature has not been practically measured, but
the nearest approach is up to 10-8 K.


Suppose a certain mass of gas having initial volume V 0 and pressure P0 at 0C is heated up
gradually at a constant volume, and again at a constant pressure separately. The corresponding
volume variation and pressure variation are found as shown in the pressure-temperature graph,

Significance of absolute zero temperature
At absolute zero temperature, the molecular motion stops, and there is no collision between gas
molecules. So, all the molecules of a gas are at complete rest at the absolute zero temperature.
Also, at the absolute zero temperature, matters are highly condensed.

13.4 Ideal Gas
Ideal gases are those having zero intermolecular force of attraction. Ideal gases strictly follow
Boyle's law and Charles' law. Ideal gas is an ideal concept. Practically, we cannot get an ideal
gas. That means each real gas deviates from the ideal gas behavior. However, at a high


temperature and a low pressure, properties of a real gas are almost similar to those of an ideal
gas. For an ideal gas, the intermolecular force of attraction must be zero, but it appears
significantly in the case of a real gas.


Ideal Gas Equation
When a certain mass of a gas changes from one equilibrium state to another equilibrium state,
its pressure, volume and temperature set up a relation between two equilibrium states on the
basis of Boyle's law and Charles' law. Hence, the ideal gas equation or equation of state is
the interrelationship between pressure, volume and temperature of the given mass of an ideal
gas on the basis of Charles’s law and Boyle’s law.

One mole is a unit for the measurement of a quantity of a substance in terms of volume or

13.6 Avogadro's Law
Statement: “Under identical condition of temperature and pressure, equal volume of all gases
contains the equal number of molecules.”
If we take 1 mole of a gas at NTP then, any gas has equal volume 22.4l = 22.4 × 10–3 m3 and
hence contains equal number of molecules 6.02 × 10 23 . For example, at NTP, 1 mole of
hydrogen gas (2 gram of hydrogen) occupies the volume of 22.4l, and contains 6.02 × 1023
molecules of hydrogen. Similarly, 1 mole of oxygen gas (32 gram of oxygen) occupies the
volume of 22.4l, and contains 6.02 × 1023 molecules of oxygen.


Avogadro's number
Avogadro's number is the number of molecules present in one mole of a gas at NTP. It is the
same for all gases, and is equal to 6.02 × 1023 molecules. It is denoted by N A. For example;
1 mole of H 2 gas contains 6.02 × 1023 H2 molecules
1 mole of O 2 gas contains 6.02 × 1023 O2 molecules, etc.
Importance of Avogadro’s Number N A
1. To calculate the number of molecules present in a given volume of gas.
2. To calculate the number of atoms present in a given amount of substance.
3. To calculate the number of molecules present in a given amount of substance.
4. To calculate the weight of one atom of an element.
5. To calculate the weight of one molecule of a substance.

13.7 Molecules, Molecular Properties of Matter and Intermolecular Force
Everything is composed of a large number of small identical particles called molecules. The
properties of such molecules determine the physical properties of a matter.

Basically, the properties of a matter are of two categories; physical properties (electrical,
magnetic, thermal, optical, acoustic, radiological mechanical, etc.), and chemical properties
(stability, reactivity, toxicity flammability, etc). Physical properties describe the interaction
between matter and energy and are measured in terms of density, temperature; viscosity, surface
tension, etc., whereas chemical properties describe the chemical response and interaction.
Physical properties explain the rearrangement of molecules whereas chemical properties explain
intra-molecular rearrangement. Therefore, generally, less energy is required to bring changes in
physical properties than in chemical properties. The intermolecular force of attraction affects
and determines the physical behavior of a matter. To understand the physical properties of a
matter it is fundamental to understand intermolecular forces.

13.8 Kinetic Molecular Model of Gases
According to the kinetic molecular model of a gas, a gas consists of a large number of
molecules. Except at absolute zero temperature, molecules are in continuous random motion
with all possible velocities. Because of random motion, the molecules collide with each other
as well as with the wall of the container. Both the collisions are elastic in nature. During
collision molecules transfer momentum to the wall of the container, therefore, according to
Newton’s law of motion, the rate of change of momentum results in the force which acts on
the wall. Also, the force acting per unit area of the wall gives pressure exerted by the gas in the
container.
Since, the diameter of a single gas molecule is very much shorter than the average separation
between the molecules, the volume of a single molecule is taken as zero. That is a molecule is
supposed to be free to move inside the container. Using this model, different laws of gas (
Charles’s, Boyle’s, etc.) are derived. This model gives ideas about the macroscopic properties
like, pressure, volume and temperature, as well as microscopic properties like kinetic energy,
velocity, mass, etc. While calculating different parameters of a gas, the kinetic molecular model
of gas uses some assumptions which are listed below.


Postulates
1. All gases are composed of a large number of perfectly small elastic spheres called molecules.
2. The attraction between gas molecules is negligible.
3. The volume of a molecule is negligible as compared to the total volume occupied by the
    gas.
4. The duration of a collision is negligible compared with the time between the collisions.

Reflection at Curved Mirror
 Born in Darmstadt, Germany on May 12, 1803, Justus von
 Liebig received his doctorate from the University of Erlangen
 in Bavaria in 1822. Justus von Liebig was a chemist, who is
 widely credited as one of the founders of agricultural
 chemistry. He made crucial contributions to the analysis of
 organic compounds, and, in his early years, also published
 several works on the use of inorganic fertilizers in several
 languages. He discovered that nitrogen was an essential plant
 nutrient, and presented his famous Law of the Minimum which
 explained the effect of individual nutrients on crops.

 A discovery by Liebig in 1835 made mirrors widely available.
 Liebig found a way to coat glass with a thin layer of metallic
 silver by depositing the metal directly by means of a chemical
 reaction.

                                                                  [Justus von Liebig, 1803-1873]
Do you know?
Convex mirrors are used in vehicles for rear view but not concave mirrors.


14.1    Introduction
Reflection of light is the fundamental concept in the study of optics and visual perception.
When light travelling through one medium approaches to the surface of another medium, it is
partly reflected, partly absorbed, and the remaining part is transmitted. "The phenomenon of
coming back of light in the same medium when it strikes on a surface is known as reflection of
light." The bouncing off of the light occurs in a predictable manner as it follows the laws of
reflection. Generally, light reflects from reflecting surfaces (plane, polished, smooth shiny
surfaces, etc.) like plane mirrors, curved mirrors, etc. The reflection of light from plane mirrors
and curved mirrors produces an image of an object. The working of optical instruments is based
on the reflection of light. The understanding of the principles of reflection of light is very
important in many aspects of the physical world around us from the functioning of our eyes to
the behavior of astronomical objects. In this chapter, we will explore the properties and
applications of reflected light establishing a found ation for further studies in physics and
applied sciences.


14.2 Image
When the reflected rays meet or appear at a point, then the image of an object is formed. There
are two types of images. They are real images and virtual images.


Real Image
An image formed due to the actual intersection of light rays after reflection or refraction is
called real image. A real image can be obtained on a screen. The real image is inverted with
respect to the object.




Virtual Image               [Fig. 14.1 (a), Real image ]
A virtual image is formed when the light rays after reflection or refraction do not actually
intersect but appear to intersect when produced backward. A virtual image cannot be obtained
on a screen. A virtual image is erected or upright with respect to the object.

   Magnification in mirrors indicates their ability to produce enlarged or reduced images. The

   a) Magnification produced by a concave mirror is used to determine the size and orientation

   b) Concave mirrors are used in various optical devices such as telescopes, microscopes,

14.6 Application of Spherical Mirrors




  Concave mirror
  i. A concave mirror in reflecting type astronomical telescopes of large aperture: A
      concave mirror is used in reflecting type astronomical telescopes of large aperture
      because a lens of a very large aperture, and free from various defects cannot be obtained
      in practice.
  ii. A concave mirror for shaving: A concave mirror is preferred to a plane mirror for
      shaving because when a person keeps his face between the pole and the focus of the
      concave mirror, an erected and highly magnified virtual image is formed. As a result, a
      proper close shaving will be possible.
  iii. A concave mirror in the ophthalmoscope: The concave mirror is used in
      ophthalmoscope so that by looking through the hole at the centre of the concave mirror,
      doctors can examine the eyes in a proper way.
  iv. The concave mirror as reflector: Concave mirrors are used as reflectors in cinema
      projectors, magic lanterns, etc. Also, the concave parabolic mirrors are used in
      searchlights.
Convex mirror in vehicles for rear view:
  A convex mirror is used in vehicles for rear view. The objects behind the vehicle are in front
  of the convex mirror so that the virtual, erected and diminished images are produced
  between the pole and the focus. This gives the clear view of the most of the rear objects to
  the driver. Thus, a convex mirror provides a much wider field of view; however, it cannot
  give the exact idea about the distance and speed of the approaching vehicle.

15.1 Introduction
Refraction of light is the fundamental concept in the field of optics which unveils the behavior
of light as it travels through different media. Refraction of light, bending of light rays as they
pass from one medium to another, plays a vital role in twinkling of stars in the night sky,
bending of straw in a glass of water, shimmering of a mirage in a desert. ThesStudy of this
fundamental phenomenon, refraction, provides a better understanding of the principles
involved in the above mentioned phenomena and the mysteries behind them. Also, the study of
refraction provides the foundation for the design of optical lenses, prisms, optical pipes, optical
fibers and many more. This chapter provides a clear picture of the refraction of light and its
influencing behaviors on our world.

15.2 Refraction of light
When a ray of light travels from one medium to another it encounters a change in density. As
a result, the velocity of light changes, and light suffers change
in initial direction in the second medium. This phenomenon is
called refraction of light. Hence, refraction is the
phenomenon of bending of light as it goes obliquely from one
medium to another.

When light encounters change in density of medium, it also suffers a change in velocity. The
change in velocity results in the change of direction of light. This change in direction of light
as it passes through a medium of varying density is called the refraction of light.


15.3 Laws of Refraction of Light
1. The incident ray, refracted ray, and normal at the point of the incident, all lie in the same
   plane.
2. When light travels from a rarer medium to a denser medium, it bends toward the normal,

This gives the critical angle for a given pair of media; water and air. Hence, the value of the
critical angle for a particular pair of media is constant, but it will be different for different pairs
of media.
If the angle of incidence in the denser medium is less than critical angle, the refraction of light
takes place in a normal way. But, if the angle of incidence is greater than the critical angle,
light undergoes total internal reflection in the same denser medium as shown in figure 15.7. In
figure, for ray of light AH,  i is greater than C and r is greater than 90. Therefore, this
is the case of total internal reflection. Hence the complete reflection of a light ray reaching an
interface with a less dense medium when the angle of incidence exceeds the critical angle is
called total internal reflection TIR. TIR occurs when the light rays travel from a more optically
denser medium to a less optically denser medium. Therefore, following are the conditions for
total internal reflection;
  1. The ray must pass from a denser medium to a rarer medium or an object must be in a denser
      medium.
  2. The angle of incidence should be greater than the critical angle.

1. Why is total internal reflection called so?
2. Light from a luminous point on the lower face of a rectangular glass slab 2.0cm thick

   the lower face. What is the refractive index of the glass?
       [1.6]


15.8.1 Mirage




                                              [Fig.15.6, Mirage formation during hot sunny
                                              day]
A mirage occurs on hot sunny days when light from distant objects undergoes total internal
reflection in the atmosphere. This creates an optical illusion where the light appears to come
from the ground, forming a virtual and inverted image just beneath the object. It's all about
how light bends in different temperatures, creating a fascinating illusion.
On a hot day, the air near the Earth's surface heats up, while the layers above cool down. This
temperature difference causes variations in air density, which affects the refractive index. As


a result, the refractive index decreases gradually from the upper layers to the lower layers.
This setup creates conditions favorable for total internal reflection of light from distant
objects.
Consider a ray, OA, from a distant object. As it passes through each layer of air, it bends
away from the normal due to refraction. Eventually, when the angle of incidence reaches the
critical angle, the ray undergoes total internal reflection, moving upward along AB. This
phenomenon creates an illusion where the distant object appears to be reflected as if it were
over a body of water.
An observer at point B sees the image of the object just below its actual position,
accompanied by a portion of the sky surrounding it. This optical illusion mimics the
appearance of an object reflected in water, creating what we perceive as a mirage.
Sample Questions:
1. Why does a black-topped road often appear to be covered with water when seen from a
   distance in summer?
2. Describe any natural phenomenon in which total internal reflection plays a part.
3. A ray of light in the air strikes a glass surface. Is there a range of angles for which total
   internal reflection takes place?
4. Can total internal reflection be achieved if an objet originates in rarer medium?

15.7 Applications of Total Internal Reflection
a. Optical Fiber:




   An optical fiber is a device based on total internal
   reflection. With the use of an optical fiber, a light
   signal can be transmitted from one place to another
   with a negligible loss of energy. It is a very long and


thin pipe (thickness nearly 10–4 m) of a transparent material with a double layer such that
the outer layer has a relatively lower refractive index. Large number of such fibers is held
together from a light pipe. Optical fibers are used for the signal for communication. A ray
of light strikes from one end at a small angle of incidence so that firstly it suffers refraction
and then multiple total internal reflections and finally strikes the other end at an angle less
than the critical angle. As a result, the ray emerges out in air as shown in figure 15.7. There
is no loss of energy during total internal reflection. The optical fiber is used in light pipe.
The application of the principle of total internal reflection in optical fibers has revolutionized
communication field, medical field, and optical examinations field. Furthermore, the optical
fiber has numerous applications as listed below.
i) Telecommunications:
     Optical fibers are extensively used in telecommunications networks to transmit voice,
     data, and video signals. High-speed and long-distance communication, telephone systems,
     and cable television are possible with the use of optical fibers. Optical fiber facilitates
     provide seamless online activities, streaming, and large file transfer.
ii) Medical Imaging:
     Optical fibers have a crucial role in medical imaging fields, such as endoscopy and fiber
     optic microscopy. Endoscopes use flexible light pipe to visualize internal organs.
iii) Data Centers:
     Optical fibers are extensively used in data centers for interconnecting servers. They are
     also used in storage systems and networking equipments. They make rapid transmission
     of large volumes of data possible.
 b. Total reflecting prism:




Total internal reflecting prism is an isosceles right-angled prism made of crown glass.
When a ray of light incident at an interface undergoes
refraction and makes an angle of incidence greater than
critical angle on other interface and it will suffer total
internal reflection as shown in figure 15.8. This type of
prism is used in binoculars and submarine periscopes.
                                                                      [Fig.15.8, Inversion by total
                                                                      internal reflection prism]


c. Sparkling of Diamond:




   The critical angle for diamond-air interface is very small, nearly 24.4. Therefore, for
   most of the cases, when light from an external source enters in a well cut diamond, it
   suffers multiple total internal reflection inside the diamond. In such situations light
   entering into diamond from all directions finally emerges out from some particular
   directions. Therefore, while looking from those directions, the diamond appears
   sparkling. A diamond cutter utilizes this principle so that multiple total internal
   reflections occur and sparkling of diamonds becomes possible.
