 Augustin-Louis Cauchy was a French mathematician and
 physicist. He was born on August 21, 1789 in Paris, France,
 and died on May 23, 1857 in Sceaux. Cauchy was one of the
 greatest of modern mathematicians. In mathematics, Cauchy
 pioneered in analysis and the theory of substitution groups.
 In optics, Cauchy defined an empirical relationship between
 the refractive index and the wavelength of light for a particular
 transparent material in 1837. This relation is called Cauchy's
 transmission equation.
 In 1816, Cauchy won the grand prix of the Institute of France
 for a paper on wave propagation which is now accepted as a
 classic in hydrodynamics. In 1822 he laid the foundations of
                                                                          Augustin- Louis Cauchy
 the mathematical theory of elasticity.                                   (21 August 1789 – 23 May 1857)
 Cauchy made substantial contributions to the theory of
 numbers and wrote three important papers on error theory. His
 work on optics provided a mathematical basis for the workable
 but somewhat unsatisfactory theory of the properties of the
 ether, a hypothetical, omnipresent medium once thought to be
 the conductor of light. His collected works, Oeuvres
 complètesd’Augustin Cauchy (1882–1970), were published in
 27 volumes.

16.1 Introduction
A prism is a seemingly simple but versatile optical tool. Study of prism provides a gateway to
a world of optical phenomena and applications of light. A prism is a simple triangular slab of
glass but it has a pivotal role in taking out the mysteries of dispersion of light, spectrum of the
rainbow, fundamental properties of light itself and many more. A prism has applications from
spectroscopy and photography to telecommunications and beyond. In this chapter we study
about the refraction of light through prism in detail.


A homogenous transparent refracting medium enclosed by two
plane surfaces meeting each other along a straight edge as
shown in figure 16.1 is called a prism. The angle between the
refracting surfaces is called the refracting angle or angle of prism.
The section cut by a plane (XYZ) perpendicular to the refracting

Hence, in this case, the angle of deviation is independent of angle of incidence but depends
upon refractive index and the angle of prism.
The advantages of totally reflecting prism over plane mirror are:
   i. Comparatively increases the intensity of image.
   ii. Does not cause the image laterally inverted.
   iii. Comparatively reduces the size of optical instrument.

Importance of Deviation through Small Angled Prism
By controlling and manipulating light precisely while passing through small angled prisms, we
can achieve desired optical performance.
    i.     Collimation and Divergence:
           A small-angle prism can cause collimation or divergence of light depending on its
           orientation. This property is used in laser beam expanders, optical metrology
           systems, etc.
    ii.     Optical Alignment:
            The deviation from a small-angled prism can be precisely controlled and measured.
            This property enables accurate alignment of optical components like lenses,
            mirrors, filters, etc. for optimal performance of optical systems.
    iii.    Dispersion Compensation:
            Small-angled prisms improve performance in fiber optics, spectroscopy and
            telecommunications by reducing chromatic dispersion.
    iv.     Image Displacement:
            Introduction a small angled prism into the optical path allows shifting of the image
            with minimal degradation. As a result, alignment of optical components, adjustment
            of path of a beam and redirecting of light in imaging systems become possible.
    v.      Prism-Based Optical Systems:
            Small angled prisms serve as fundamental components in optical systems like
            telescopes, binoculars, and periscopes to create complex functions such as image
            rotation, light path manipulation, etc.

17.1 Introduction
Lens is a homogenous transparent medium enclosed by two spherical refracting surfaces.
Lenses are commonly used in our daily life. For example, eyeglasses, contact lenses, cameras,
smartphones, microscopes, binoculars, telescopes, projectors, reading glasses, magnifying
glasses, headlights, spotlights and flashlights of vehicles, eyepieces in binoculars and


microscopes, etc. Lenses are essential optical components that enable us to see objects and
images clearly, capture images, explore the world around us, and enhance our visual
experiences in various ways. There are mainly two types of lenses; concave and convex.




1. Convex Lens
A lens thicker in the middle and thinner at the edges as shown in figure 17.1 is called a convex
lens. There are of three types convex lenses.
Bi-convex lens: A lens having both
surfaces convex as shown in figure
17.2 (i) is a bi-convex lens. Radii of
curvatures of two surfaces may or
may not be equal.
Plano-convex lens: A lens having
one surface plane and the other
surface convex as shown in figure 17.2 (ii) a plano-convex lens.
                               [Fig.17.1, A convex lens]   [Fig. 17.2, Types of convex lenses]
Concavo - convex lens: It is a lens having one surface concave and the other convex as shown
in figure 17.2(iii). For this lens radius of curvature of the convex surface is less than that of the
concave surface.


2. Concave Lens
A lens which is thinner in the middle
and thicker at the edges as shown in
figure 17.3 is called a concave lens.
Concave lenses are of three types.

       [Fig.17.3, A concave lens][Fig.17.4, Types of concave lenses]


Bi-concave lens: A lens having both surfaces concave as shown in figure 17.4 (i) is a bi-
concave lens. Radii of curvatures of two surfaces may or may not be equal.
Plano-concave lens: It is a lens having one surface plane and the other surface concave as shown
in figure 17.4 (ii).
Convexo – concave lens: It is a lens having one surface convex and the other concave as shown
in figure 17.4 (iii). The radius of curvature of the concave surface is less than that of the convex
surface.

Properties of Spherical Lenses
The properties of lenses determine their optical behavior. Therefore, it is important to
understand the properties of spherical lenses for their proper design, and for using them in
various applications effectively to ensure proper focus, image clarity, and optical performance.
Important properties of spherical lenses are explained below.
Focal Length (f): It is the distance between the optical centre and the principal focus of a lens.
The focal length determines the conversing as well as the diverging power of a lens. A lens
with a shorter focal length has a stronger converging power whereas a lens with a longer focal
length has a weaker converging power.
Optical Power (P): The optical power is the measure of the ability of a lens to bend (converse
or diverge) the rays of light. It is expressed as reciprocal to the focal length so that the focal
                                                                1
length must be in meter. Therefore, the power of lens, P = . A lens with a higher optical
                                                                f
power bends the light more strongly than a lens with a lower optical power.
Shape of Lens: Spherical lenses have a characteristic shape. One or both the surfaces of a
spherical lens are the portions of a sphere. The shape of a lens may be concave or convex.
Aperture: The aperture of a lens is the effective diameter of the lens through which light
   passes. The amount of light that can enter the lens depends on its aperture. It also affects the
   brightness of the image formed.

Principal axis: The line joining the centers of curvature of the two refracting surfaces of a
lens is called the principal axis (C 1 C2 ).
Principal focus (F): A point on the principal axis is such a point, where all the rays parallel
to the principal axis intersect after refraction through a convex lens. In case of a concave
lens, the rays of light appear to come from the principal focus. Every lens has two principal
foci, one for each refracting surface. The foci of a convex lens are real and the foci of the
concave lens are virtual.
Optical centre (O): The optical centre of the lens is its geometrical centre from where the
rays of the light pass without deviation. It is denoted by O.
Focal length (f): The distance between the optical centre and the principal focus of a lens is
called its focal length. It is denoted by f. The focal length of convex lenses is taken as
positive, and that of concave lenses is taken as negative.
Focal plane: The plane passing through the focus and which is perpendicular to the principal
axis of a lens is called the focal plane.
Centre of curvature: Lenses are formed by the combination of two curved surfaces. Those
curved surfaces are the parts of two spheres. The centers of those spheres are called centers
of curvature of the lens. Therefore, a lens has two centers of curvature. In figure 17.5, C1
and C2 are centers of curvature.
Radius of curvature: The radius of the sphere of which a part is a lens is called the radius
of curvature. A lens has two radii of curvature R 1 and R2 . The radii of curvature of convex
lenses are taken as positive, and that of concave lenses are taken as negative.


17.2    Sign Conventions of Lens
The sign convention is a bunch of rules to set signs for different distances like image distance,
object distance, focal length, etc. in ray diagrams of spherical lenses for the mathematical
analysis of an image formation.
Sign conventions for the lens are given below:
  i. The aperture of the lens is small.
 ii. All the distances are measured from the optical centre of the lens.
iii. All the distances of real objects and real images are taken as positive whereas all the
         distances of virtual objects and virtual images are taken as negative.
iv. Convex lenses can form both real and virtual images but concave lenses can form only virtual
         images.
 v. Focal length and radius of the curvature of a convex lens are taken as positive whereas those
         for a concave lens are taken as negative.

17.6 Power of a Lens
Do you know why some people in your locality use spectacles?
Do you know the power of the lens they used in their spectacles?


Every ray of light falling on the convex lens deviates towards the principal axis and tends to
converge, but every ray of light falling on the concave lens deviates away from the principal
axis and tends to diverge. Therefore, the main function of the lens is to deviate the light rays
incident on it and hence power of a lens is measured in terms of its ability to deviate the rays.

The ability of a lens to converge or diverge a ray of light after refraction through it is
called the power of that lens. It is defined as the reciprocal of focal length. A lens of a short
focal length produces more deviation than
that of a lens of a larger focal length as

Dispersion
 Augustin-Jean Fresnel was a French civil engineer and physicist.
 Fresnel pioneered in optics and did much to establish
 the wave theory of light advanced by English physicist Thomas
 young.
 Fresnel presented his work on diffractionin 1819. A
 mathematician Simeon-Denis Poisson (a prominent advocate of
 Newton’s corpuscular model of light) pointed out that Fresnel’s
 model predicted a different result: when a parallel beam of light
 falls on a small spherical obstacle, there will be a bright spot at
 the centre of the circular shadow. The spot was nearly as bright
 as if the obstacle was not there at all. An experiment performed      Augustin-Jean Fresnel
 by the French physicist Aragoand validated that spot
                                                                       (10 May 1788 – 14 July 1827)
 (subsequently called Poisson’s spot).

3. How and in which situation does a rainbow appear in the sky?
4. Why white light splits into different colours?




18.1 Introduction
The dispersion of light is an important phenomenon in the field of optics, which provides the
spectrum of colors that forms the essence of our visual world. When white light encounters a
medium like a prism or a droplet of water, its composite wavelengths undergo a mesmerizing
transformation, and give an array of colors ranging from violet to red, each representing a
unique wavelength of light. This phenomenon is known as dispersion, and it was famously
demonstrated by Isaac Newton in the 17th century. The study of dispersion explores the secrets
behind rainbows, colour spectrum from prisms, and a number of natural phenomena.


18.2 Dispersion of light
                                             A




                                       P



                               B
                                                     C
                               [Fig.18.1, Dispersion of light through a glass prism]


When a beam of white light falls on the refracting face of a prism, it splits into seven colours
as shown in figure 18.1. Those seven colours are violet, indigo, blue, green, yellow, orange,
and red. The band of seven colours obtained on the screen is called the spectrum of white light.
The phenomenon is called the dispersion of light. Therefore, dispersion of light is defined as
the phenomenon of splitting white light into its constituent colors. The formation of a
rainbow is an example of the dispersion of light.


18.3 Cause of Dispersion
The refractive index of a medium is highly colour dependent. It is inversely proportional to the
                                                                        B     c
wave length of the light (from Cauchy’s empirical relation = A+ 2 + 4 + ......). Since, the
                                                                        λ    λ
wave length of orange light is smaller than that of red light, the refractive index of red colour
r is less than that of orange colour o . Similarly, the refractive index of yellow light is less
than that of orange light and so on. Therefore from the relation  = A ( – 1),
v >i>b >g>y >o >r. That is different colour of light deviate along different directions with
different values of angle of deviation. Therefore, when white light is incident on a refracting
face of a prism, different colours are refracted through different angles. As a result, a white
light splits and dispersion takes place.


Results of dispersion of light
a. Rainbow
   The natural phenomenon of dispersion of light is the
   dispersion of sunlight in the sky which gives a rainbow
   formation. Rainbow is a natural spectrum which is seen
   in the sky. During rainfall, a rain drop behaves as a
   dispersive medium like a prism, and the sky acts as
   screen so that at a particular and suitable angle of
   incidence, a white ray of light incident on rain drop
   splits into its seven constituent colours, and a rainbow is
   seen in the sky.
                                                                  [Fig. 18.2 Rainbow formation]


b. Blue colour of sky
      The sky looks blue due to the dispersion of light
      followed by scattering. When sunlight passes through
      the atmosphere it suffers dispersion. Also,it suffers
      scattering from dust particles and air molecules.
      According to Rayleigh empirical formula of scatterin is
                                 1
      g (scattering intensity  4 ). Red light scatters least,
                                 λ
      and blue light scatters most. The blue colour, which
      scatters most, covers the sky. Due to this the sky seems blue.                 [Fig.18.3
      Blue sky due to dispersion]

c. Sun appears red during Sunrise and Sun-set
      The Sun light suffers dispersion during its long
      travel through the atmosphere. During sunrise or
      sunset, when the Sun is close to the horizon, the
      light must travel a longer distance through the
      atmosphere than it does when the Sun is overhead.
      This results in comparatively more scattering of
      light. Red colour scatters the least, and becomes
      capable to reach our eyes, but other colours scatter
      away. Hence, during sunset and sunrise the sun
      appears red.
                                [Fig.18.4 Red appearance of the sky due to dispersion of light]

18.4   Spectrum of Light
The band of seven colors obtained, when a white light splits into its constituent colors on
striking the surface of a glass prism is called a spectrum." In other words, a spectrum is a
collection of dispersed light that gives wavelength composition. When white light is incident
on a prism, it is splitted into different constituent colours which are deviated through different
angles. Such dispersed light, when received on the screen or photographic plate, forms a
spectrum. There are two types of spectrum; pure spectrum and impure spectrum.
Pure Spectrum
When the white light is dispersed through a glass prism, and split colours do not overlap to
each other (all colors can be seen distinctly) on the screen as shown in figure 18.2, then the
corresponding spectrum is pure spectrum of light. A better method of obtaining a pure spectrum
is to use a parallel beam of light as in an instrument called a spectrometer. For this an
illuminated slit is placed at the principal focus of a converging lens so that a parallel beam of
light emerges from it, and falls on a prism. Refraction through the prism splits up the light into


         separate parallel beams of different colours, each of which is brought to its own focus in the
         focal plane of a second lens. The resulted pure spectrum may be formed on a white screen, or
         can be viewed through a magnifying eyepiece. Therefore, for obtaining pure spectrum
         following conditions should be satisfied.
             1. Slit should be narrow.
             2. Rays coming out from convex lens should have parallel incidence.
             3. Prism should be in condition of minimum deviation.
             4. Emerging light rays should be focused by achromatic lens.

18.7    Aberration of Light in Lenses
The deviation in the shape, size and position of the actual image from the image predicted by
lens formula is called aberration. It is defined as a property of optical systems such as lenses
that causes light to be spread out over some region of space rather than being focused to a point.
An optical system with aberration will produce a blurred image that is not sharp, and cannot be
seen with clarity. There are different types of aberration; Chromatic aberration, Spherical
aberration, etc.
a. Chromatic Aberration
A lens may be considered as the combination of prisms so it exhibits
prismatic behavior. If rays of light parallel with the principal axis incident
on the surface of the lens then they split up into different constituent colours
after refraction. "An inability of a lens to focus all colours of light at a
single point on the principal axis is called chromatic aberration. It is also
known as axial or longitudinal aberration. The chromatic aberration is
measured in terms of the difference in focal lengths of red colour (f r) and
violet colour (f v ).

b. Spherical Aberration in a Lens
Spherical aberration is an inability of a lens to focus the paraxial rays and marginal rays at the
same point on the principal axis. The spherical aberration of the lens is due to its spherical
shape. The rays passing through the lens close to its centre (paraxial rays) are focused farther
away than rays passing through a circular zone near its rim (marginal rays). Images formed by
the lens having large apertures are therefore not sharp but get sharper at smaller apertures.
Spherical aberration is found in case of near objects and it is positive for the convex lens and
negative for the concave lens.

Consider a pointed object (O) has been placed on the principal axis of convex lens L so that
paraxial rays from O are focused at point I p (longer distance) whereas marginal rays are focused
at point I m(shorter distance) on the other side of the lens. The image is not sharp at any point
on the axis. If the screen is placed perpendicular to the axis, then the image appears as a circular
patch of diameter AB as shown in figure 18.9. The spherical aberration in the convex lens is
shown in figure 18.10.
To remove spherical aberration in a lens, essentially its focal length for each zone must be
made equal so that refracted rays meet at the same point. Practically it is impossible. Therefore,
the spherical aberration in a lens can only be reduced but cannot be removed completely.

Applications of Achromatism in Lens
      Achromatism refers to the ability of the lens system to minimize or eliminate chromatic
      aberration. Achromatic lenses are designed for the correction of chromatic aberration, and
      so that it ensures different colors of light to converge at a single focal point.
      Achromaticlenses are essential in a wide range of applications such as photography to
      astronomy for accurate color correction and high-quality imaging. By minimizing
      chromatic aberration, achromatic lenses can improve image clarity, color accuracy, and
      precision and reliability of optical performance. Some applications of achromatism in
      lenses are explained below.


i) Camera Lenses in photography: Achromatic lenses are widely used in camera to produce
     high-quality images with minimal chromatic aberration. The combination helps to
     converge all colours of light at the same focal point so that sharp and clear images are
     obtained.
ii) Optical Systems: Achromatic lenses are in many optical systems such as binoculars,
     spotting scopes, range finders, surveying instruments, spectrometers to obtain accurate and
     color-corrected images. As a result, we achieve precise optical performance.
iii)Optical Fiber Systems: Achromatic lenses are used in optical fiber systems to improve the
     transmission of signals by maintaining the integrity of the optical signal travelling through
     optical fiber. This makes improvement in performance and reliability of the communication
     system.
iv) Projector Systems: Achromatic lenses are used in projector systems such as overhead
     projectors, digital projectors, etc. to ensure the accurate focus and color reproduction to
     obtain sharp images.

text:
Electric Charges




Charles Coulomb, French physicist (1736–1806)
Coulomb’s major contributions to science were in the areas of electrostatics and magnetism.
During his lifetime, he also investigated the strengths of materials, and determined the forces
that affect objects on beams, thereby contributing to the field of structural mechanics. In the
field of ergonomics, his research provided a fundamental understanding of the ways in which
people and animals can work the best.
You can receive a mildly unpleasant shock, and produce a little spark if you touch a metal
doorknob after walking across a carpet. Vigorously brushing your freshly washed hair makes
all the hairs fly apart. A plastic comb that you’ve run through your hair will pick up bits of
paper and other small objects, but a metal comb won’t. The common factor in these
observations is that two objects are rubbed together. Why should rubbing an object cause forces
and sparks? What kind of forces are these? Why do metallic objects behave differently from
nonmetallic? These are the questions with which we begin our study of electricity.
19.1 Introduction
Everyday objects contain an enormous number of charged particles, and they usually have an
equal number of positive charges (protons) and negative charges (electrons), so that they have
no overall charge, and are therefore described as being neutral. Negatively charged electrons
are the outermost particles in atoms and some of them are not tightly bound to atoms. If
electrons can be added to, or removed from, a neutral object, it will then have an overall charge
and we describe the object as being charged, which can then result in electrostatic effects.
Protons, unlike electrons, are located in the nuclei of atoms and cannot be separated or moved
from their positions, so they are not involved in producing electrostatic effects.


If a neutral object is given excess electrons, it becomes negatively charged. If the number of
electrons is reduced, the object becomes positively charged.
19.2 Charging by friction
One common example is seen in Figure 19.1, when brushing dry hair with a plastic brush,
electrons can be transferred in the process, one object (the hair brush) gains electrons, becoming
negatively charged, while removing electrons from the other object (the hair), leaving it with a
positive charge.




               Fig. 19.1
The two objects will then attract each other. In this example, individual hairs with similar
charge can also be seen to be repelled from each other.
 In school experiments, in order to produce electrostatics effects, insulating rods are often
rubbed with cloths. Depending on the materials, one will become positively charged, and the
other negatively charged, as electrons are transferred between the rod and the cloth. These
insulating materials have much fewer mobile charge carriers (free electrons) than metals, but
if metals were used, the charges would not stay in the same place.
 When friction occurs between substances, electrons are often transferred between their
surfaces.
19.3 Charging by Induction
If you bring a charged object near a conducting surface, electrons are made to move in the
surface material, even without physical contact.




                                       Fig. 19.2
Consider the two insulated metal spheres, A and B, in the figures above. In part 19.2 (a), the
spheres touch each other, so in effect they form a single uncharged conductor. In part (b),
when a negatively charged rod is brought near A, electrons in the metal, being free to move,


are repelled as far as possible until their mutual repulsion is strong enough to balance the
influence of the rod: The charge is redistributed. In parts (c) and (d), if the spheres are
separated while the rod is still present, each will be equally and oppositely charged. This is
charging by induction. The charged rod has never touched the spheres, and the rod retains the
same charge it had initially.
Activities:
   1. Charge a plastic rod by rubbing it with wool. Touch a neutral metal sphere with the
      rubbed area of the rod. The metal sphere then picks up small pieces of paper and
      repels a charged, hanging plastic rod. The metal sphere appears to have acquired
      “plastic charge.”




                                     Fig. 19.3
   2. Charge a plastic rod, then run your finger along it. After you’ve done so, the rod no
      longer picks up small pieces of paper or repels a charged, hanging plastic rod.
      Similarly, the metal sphere of Experiment 1 no longer repels the plastic rod after you
      touch it with your finger.




                                    Fig. 19.4
   3. Place two metal spheres close together with a plastic rod connecting them. Charge a
      second plastic rod, by rubbing, and touch it to one of the metal spheres. Afterward,
      the metal sphere that was touched picks up small pieces of paper and repels a charged,
      hanging plastic rod. The other metal sphere does neither.




                                     Fig. 19.5

       Our experiments have shown that charge can be transferred from one object to another,
       but only when the objects touch. Contact is required. Removing charge from an object,
       which you can do by touching it, is called discharging.

       There are two types or classes of materials with very different electric properties. We
       call these conductors and insulators.


19.4 Coulomb’s law for the electric force
In physics, fields are regions in which an object will experience a force at a distance. An electric
(or electrostatic) field is created by charged objects. Other charged objects in this electric field
will experience force.
The electric force between two electric charges, 𝑄1 and 𝑄2 , was investigated in 1785 by Charles
Augustin Coulomb (1736–1806).
Coulomb discovered that the electric force between two point charges is inversely proportional
to the square of the separation of the charges, and is proportional to the product of the two
charges. It is attractive for charges of opposite sign, and repulsive for charges of the same sign.
Mathematically,

If we have a positive and a negative charge, then the force F is negative. We interpret this as an

So far, we have considered point charges. If we are considering uniformly charged spheres we
measure the distance from the centre of one to the centre of the other – they behave as if their

text:
Electric field
Karl Friedrich Gauss, German mathematician and astronomer (1777–1855)




German mathematician and astronomer (1777–1855) Gauss received a doctoral degree in
mathematics from the University of Helmstedt in 1799. In addition to his work in
electromagnetism, he made contributions to mathematics and science in number theory,
statistics, non-Euclidean geometry, and cometary orbital mechanics. He was the founder of the
German Magnetic Union, which studies the Earth’s magnetic field continually.
20.1 Introduction
In physics, fields are regions in which an object will experience a force at a distance. An electric
(or electrostatic) field is created by charged objects. Other charged objects in this electric field
will experience force. You can create an electric field very easily by rubbing a glass rod with a
silk cloth. Friction transfers electrons from the glass to the silk, making the cloth negative, and
the rod positive. The rod is then surrounded by an electric field — it will attract small pieces
of paper or water from a dripping tap.
Nature creates its own electric fields. The strong electric field between the base of a
thundercloud and the ground helps to channel the electric current of lightning.
   1. Electric charge, Q, is measured in coulombs (C), and can be either positive or negative.
   2. Oppositely charged particles attract each other. Like charges repel.
   3. If a charged object is placed in an electric field, then it will experience a force.
   4. If the charged object is a sphere, you can assume that all of its charges is at its centre.
   5. Just like gravitational fields, electric fields can be represented by field lines
20.2 Electric field lines
Sometimes, the origin of a force between two objects is obvious, an example is the friction pad
in a brake rubbing on the rim of a bicycle wheel to slow the cycle down. In other cases, there
is no physical contact between two objects yet a force exists between them. Examples include
the magnetic force between two magnets and the electrostatic force between two charged
objects. Such forces are said to “act at a distance”.


The term field is used in physics for cases where two separated objects exert forces on each
other. We say that in the case of the comb picking up the paper, the paper is sitting in the electric
field due to the comb. The concept of the field is an extremely powerful one in physics not least
because there are many ideas common to all fields.
Any two charged objects exert equal and opposite forces on each other without being directly
in contact. An electric field is said to surround each charge. Suppose a small positive charge is
placed as a test charge near a body with a much bigger charge which is also positive. If the test
charge is free to move, it will follow a path away from the body with the bigger charge. The
path a free positive test charge follows is called a line of force or a field line.
 The field lines of an electric field are the lines which the positive test charges follow. The
direction of an electric field line is the direction a positive test charge would move along.
The idea of field lines was first introduced by Michael Faraday. Although the field lines are
imaginary, they are useful for illustrating and understanding the nature of a particular field.
There are some conventions for drawing these electric field patterns.
The lines start and end on charges of opposite signs.
An arrow is essential to show the direction in which a positive charge would move (i.e. away
from the positive charge and towards the negative charge).
Where the field is strong, the lines are close together. The lines act to repel each other.
The lines never cross.
The lines meet a conducting surface at 90°.
Figure 20.1 shows the patterns of the field around different charged objects.




Field lines due to a charged sphere


Field lines due to dipole




Field lines due to a uniform field




Field lines due to a positive charge close to a conductor.




Fig. 20.1
Field lines between oppositely charged parallel plates.
Experiments suggest that the field between two parallel plates is uniform in the region
between the plates and becomes weaker at the edges (these are known as edge effects).
At the edge, the field lines curve outwards as the field gradually weakens from the large value
between the plates to the much weaker field well away from them.
Radial electric fields
The electric field between two parallel charged plates is uniform; what shape of electric field
does a small ‘point’ charge like a single proton produce?
 An isolated positive charge P produces an electric field like that shown in Figure 20.2. The
radial lines of force show the direction of the field around P.




               Fig. 20.2


Of course, the electric field lines spread out in three dimensions from the charge – the
diagram only shows them in two dimensions.
The arrows on the lines of force would be reversed if the charge were negative. Equipotential
lines in this case will be drawn as circles, but in three dimensions they will be spherical
surfaces.
A charged sphere, or even an almost-spherical charged head, also produces a radial field.
Figure 20.3 confirms this as the boy’s hair shows clearly the direction of the electric field
around his head.




Fig. 20.3


20.3 Electric field strength
The electric field strength is defined using the concept of a positive test charge.
The electric field strength, E, at a point in the field, is defined as the force per unit charge on a
positive test charge placed at that point.

is at point P, a distance r away from the isolated charge. We put another charge, a positive test

20.6 Gauss’s Law
Gauss’s law is based on the inverse-square behavior of the electric force between point
charges. Although Gauss’s law is a consequence of Coulomb’s law, it is more convenient for
calculating the electric fields of highly symmetric charge distributions, and makes it possible
to deal with complicated problems using qualitative reasoning.


                                                   Fig. 20.12: Three imaginary boxes are
                                                   constructed of a material that does not affect
                                                   electric fields. A positive test charge is
                                                   brought up to the box from the left toward: (a)
                                                   an empty box; (b) a box with a positive charge
inside; (c) a box with a negative charge inside.


To begin our discussion of Gauss’s Law, let’s imagine a box in the shape of a cube (Figure a),
which is constructed of a material that does not affect electric fields. A positive test charge
brought close to any surface of the box will experience no force. Now, suppose a positive
charge is inside the box and the positive test charge is brought close to the surface of the box
(Figure b). The positive test charge experiences an outward force due to the positive charge
inside the box. If the test charge is close to any surface of the box, it experiences the outward
force. If twice as much positive charge is inside the box, the positive test charge experiences
twice the outward force when brought close to any surface of the box.
Now, suppose there is a negative charge inside the box (Figure c). When the positive test charge
is brought close to one surface of the box, the charge experiences an inward force. If the positive
test charge is close to any surface of the box, it experiences an inward force. Doubling the
negative charge in the box doubles the inward force on the test charge when it is close to any
surface of the box.
In an analogy with flowing water, the electric field lines seem to be flowing out of the box
containing positive charge and into the box containing negative charge.
Now, let’s imagine an empty box in a uniform electric field (Figure 20.13).


                     Fig 20.13: Imaginary empty box in a uniform electric field.


If a positive test charge is brought close to side 1, it experiences an inward force. If the charge
is close to side 2, it experiences an outward force. The electric field is parallel to the other four
sides, so the positive test charge does not experience any inward or outward force when brought
close to those sides. Thus, in the analogy with flowing water, the net amount of electric field
that seems to be flowing in and out of the box is zero. Whenever a charge is inside the box, the
electric field lines seem to be flowing in or out of the box. When there is no charge in the box,
the net flow of electric field lines in or out of the box is zero.
These observations and the definition of electric flux, which quantifies the concept of the
flow of the electric field lines, lead to Gauss’s Law:

Here, q is the net charge inside a closed surface, called a Gaussian surface. The closed surface
could be a box like that we have been discussing or any arbitrarily shaped closed surface.


Usually, the shape of the Gaussian surface is chosen so as to reflect the symmetries of the
problem situation.
Gauss’s law can be stated as ‘the electric flux 𝜙 through any closed surface is equal to the net
charge inside the surface, 𝑞 inside, divided by 𝜀0 .’

Gauss’s law, is one of four fundamental relations that govern the behavior of electromagnetic
fields throughout the universe. Whether you journey into a star in some remote galaxy, down
among the strands of a DNA molecule, or into the microprocessor chip at the heart of your
computer, you’ll find that the flux of the electric field through any closed surface depends only
on the enclosed charge. In nearly 200 years of experiments, no electric field has ever been
found to violate Gauss’s law.

21.1 Electrical Potential
The electric potential at a point is the work done in bringing a unit positive test charge from
infinity to the point.
                         work done in moving charge between two points 𝑊

The energy stored in the system per unit charge is what we call the potential of the system.
If we have two charges of opposite sign, then they attract each other, and the situation is
exactly the same as in gravitation. In other words, when the charges are some finite distance
apart, energy is required to move them to infinite separation. As the charges separate, the
electric potential will gradually climb to zero.
The situation changes when the two charges have the same sign: now both charges repel each
other.
Imagine two negative charges held at some finite distance apart. Energy was stored in the
system when the charges were brought together from infinity. If they are released, the two
charges will fly apart (to infinity where the repulsive force becomes zero). The system does
work on the charges. There must have been a positive amount of energy stored in the system
before the charges were allowed to separate. The potential is still defined to be zero at
infinity, but this time as one charge is moved from infinity towards the other charge, the
overall value of the potential rises above the zero level to become positive. Work has been
done on the charge.

21.5 Potential Gradients
The electric potential can be represented by drawing equipotential lines or, in three dimensions,
equipotential surfaces. An equipotential surface is one on which all points are at the same
potential. That is, the potential difference between any two points on the surface is zero, so no
work is required to move a charge from one point on the surface to the other. An equipotential
surface must be perpendicular to the electric field at any point.
Equipotentials are surfaces of constant potential. A test charge moving along a line on an
equipotential surface has constant potential energy. No work is done by the electric field on the
test charge because the force due to the field is at right angles to the equipotential. In other
words, the lines of force of the electric field cross an equipotential surface at right angles (ie.
along the normal). The equipotentials for an electric field are like equipotentials for a
gravitational field. Both are lines of constant potential energy for the appropriate test object, in
one case a test charge, and in the other case a test mass.

21.7 Similarities between Electric and Gravitation Fields
A comparison between Newton’s law of gravitation and Coulomb’s law shows that there are
many similarities between the actions of the two types of force. There are also some important
differences.
The main similarities are as follows:
   i) Both electric and gravitational forces are non-contact; forces are exerted over a distance
        without direct contact.
   ii) Both forces are of infinite range.
   iii) Both forces obey inverse square laws.
The main differences are as follows:
   i) Gravitational forces between masses are always attractive; electric forces can be
        attractive or repulsive.
   ii) An electric force is much stronger than the gravitational force.
   iii) It is possible to shield an electric force, but the gravitational force acts on all objects.
   iv) An electric force only acts on charged objects; the gravitational force acts on all
        objects.

Capacitors
Look at the pictures. Have you ever noticed these electrical components in any
electrical/electronic devices? Why are they so important in electronics?




                                    Fig. 22.1


22.1 Introduction
Capacitors are components of electrical circuits that temporarily store electric charge. They are
electrical components in which charge is separated. They come in a variety of shapes and sizes.
However, their basic construction is the same.
 A capacitor consists of two metallic plates separated from each other by an insulator (often
known as a dielectric) such as air, paper, ceramic, or mica. The circuit symbol for a capacitor
shows two lines separated by a gap). You can easily make your own capacitor from two sheets
of aluminium foil separated by newspaper.




               Fig. 22.2


22.2 Storing charge
Figure 22.3 shows a capacitor connected to a cell of e.m.f. E.




       Fig. 22.3


When the capacitor is connected to the cell, electrons flow from the cell for a very short time.
They cannot travel between the plates because of the insulation. The very brief current means
electrons are removed from plate A of the capacitor, and at the same time electrons are
deposited onto the other plate B. Plate A becomes deficient in electrons, that is, it acquires a
net positive charge. Plate B gains electrons and hence acquires a negative charge. The current
in the circuit must be the same at all points and charge must be conserved, so the two plates
have an equal but opposite charge of magnitude Q. Therefore, there is a potential difference
(p.d.) across the plates. The current in the circuit falls to zero when the p.d. across the plates
is equal to the e.m.f. E of the cell. The capacitor is then fully charged. The net charge on the
capacitor plates is zero.
The capacitor is therefore really a device that separates electrical charge into —Q and +Q.


23.3 Capacitance
If a voltage is applied across a capacitor by connecting the capacitor to a battery with
conducting wires as in figure22.6, the two plates quickly become charged: one plate acquires
a negative charge, the other an equal amount of positive charge. Each battery terminal and the
capacitor plate connected to it are at the same potential. Hence the full battery voltage
appears across the capacitor.




       Fig. 22.6
 For a given capacitor, it is found that the amount of charge Q acquired by each plate is
proportional to the magnitude of the potential difference V between the plates:
                                             𝑄 = 𝐶𝑉

The constant of proportionality, C, in Eq. is called the capacitance of the capacitor.
The ability of any object to store charge is called capacitance. Capacitance is given the
symbol C, and the SI unit is the farad (F). Commercial capacitors are usually marked with
their capacitance value, which indicates the amount of charge Q that the capacitor can store
for a given p.d. V.
The capacitance of a capacitor is defined as the charge stored per unit p.d. across it. That is;

For any capacitor, the greater the amount of positive and negative charge stored on the two
plates, the greater the p.d. across them, so the charge on the capacitor is always proportional to
the p.d.
The unit of capacitance is the coulomb per volt, or farad (symbol: F) and is named after Michael
Faraday, the English physicist. In fundamental units the farad is equivalent to A 2 S4 kg–1 m–2.
One farad is a very large unit of capacitance since 1 C of charge is a very large amount of
charge and you will usually use capacitances measured in mill farads (mF), microfarads (µF),
and Pico farads (pF).

A graph of charge stored, Q, against pd, V from measurements, is shown in figure 22.7. A
straight line is passing through the origin. Therefore, the charge stored, Q, is proportional to
the pd, V. In other words, the charge stored per volt is constant.

22.4 Parallel-Plate Capacitor
The arrangement of parallel plates in which the two plates are separated by an insulator is called
a parallel plate capacitor. The insulator might be a vacuum, it could also be air or another gas
or it could also be a non-conducting material such as a plastic.
The capacitance of a parallel-plate capacitor depends on the area of the plates, their distance
apart and the ability of the insulating material between the plates to separate the charge, a
property known as permittivity.
The permittivity of a material is the resistance of the material to an electric field passing through
it. If the permittivity is high, then a larger charge can be stored on the plates for any given
potential difference across them. The permittivity of capacitor insulating materials is always
measured relative to the permittivity of free space (vacuum), 𝜀0 , using a relative permittivity,
𝜀𝑟 , sometimes called the dielectric constant of the material. The total absolute permittivity of
an insulator is therefore given by the product 𝜀𝑟 𝜀0 . The permittivity of free space is 𝜀0 =
8.85 × 10−12 𝐹𝑚−1 .

Materials used for the dielectric include; paper, mica (a mineral that can be cut into thin layers),
Teflon, plastics, ceramics, and the oxides of various metals such as aluminium.

22.5 Dielectric Strength of Dielectrics
If the potential difference across a capacitor is increased, a maximum field strength will be
reached after which the dielectric becomes a conductor. A spark will then jump between the
plates. This maximum field is called the dielectric strength of the dielectric. For air this is about
1 kV mm-1 (the exact value depends on temperature, pressure, and how dry the air is); for Teflon
the dielectric strength is 60 kVmm-1 . If during thunderstorms the electric field strength in air
between charged clouds or between a charged cloud and the ground exceeds this critical value,
then a lightning strike may occur.
If a material between the plates replaces the air (or vacuum), the new material can do two things
for the capacitor designer: it can be used to separate the plates by a fixed amount, and also
change the properties of the capacitor at the same time.
As we know materials have their own permittivity which is greater than that of a vacuum. To
treat this mathematically, when a material of permittivity ε is present we replace ε0 in the
equations where it occurs with ε alone. The values for ε are different for different materials.


A useful thing happens when a dielectric material is inserted between capacitor plates to fill all
the space between them. A dielectric is an electrical insulator that is polarized when placed in
an electric field. The origin of the polarization is in the molecules of the dielectric substance.
Each molecule is slightly more positive at one end than the other. This means that when a
molecule is in an electric field, it responds either by moving slightly or by rotating so that the
more positive end of the molecule moves in the direction of the electric field. If the molecules
are in a solid and the solid is packed between the plates of a capacitor then this reduces the
electric field strength between the plates.




                Fig. 22.8
When the dielectric is in place (Fig. 22.8), the molecules inside it respond to the field produced
by the capacitor. Notice the field directions carefully. In the diagram, the original field 𝐸𝑐𝑎𝑝 of
the capacitor is from right to left, but the dielectric field 𝐸dielectric (indicated by the charges at
the surface of the dielectric) is from left to right. Therefore, the net field between the plates is
equal to the capacitor field minus the dielectric field. The overall field 𝐸𝑛𝑒𝑡 in the dielectric is
                                                           𝑉
reduced, and because 𝐸𝑛𝑒𝑡 = 𝐸𝑐𝑎𝑝 − 𝐸dielectric = 𝑑 (𝑉 𝑖𝑠 𝑡ℎ𝑒 𝑝𝑜𝑡𝑒𝑛𝑡𝑖𝑎𝑙 𝑑𝑖𝑓𝑓𝑒𝑟𝑒𝑛𝑐𝑒) V
also decreases as d is fixed. The insertion of the dielectric reduces the potential difference
between the plates because some of the stored energy of the capacitor has been used to align
                                                                          𝑄
the dielectric molecules. The overall charge stored is unchanged, so, 𝑉 is increased, and hence
so is the capacitance of the capacitor. Dielectrics increase the capacitance of a capacitor.
Another way to describe the action of the dielectric is by saying that the presence of the
dielectric raises the potential of the negative plate and lowers the potential of the positive plate;
this reduces the potential difference between the plates.
This explanation of the dielectric effect is a simplified one. There are other reasons for the
increase in capacitance, but in many cases the explanation can be given in terms of potential
change as here.


                               Fig. 22.9
Figure 22.9 (a) shows some typical designs used for practical capacitors. A very common
type of capacitor is the electrolytic capacitor shown as a cutaway in figure 22.9 (b). The
designer here uses the dielectric advantageously by using it to space the two metal foils apart.
The capacitor layers are then rolled up together (rather like rolling up three carpets initially
on top of each other). This type of capacitor must be connected into a circuit correctly. The
dielectric material is a chemical (the electrolyte in the diagram) that is a good dielectric when
the electric field direction is correct. In this design the layers are very thin (good because d is
small) and the plate area is large (even better) giving some of the largest values of
capacitance possible in a given volume.
Materials used for the dielectric include; paper, mica (a mineral that can be cut into thin
layers), Teflon, plastics, ceramics, and the oxides of various metals such as aluminium.
Workedout Example
In a laboratory experiment, two parallel plates, each of area 100 cm2 , are separated by 1.5 cm.
Calculate the capacitance of the arrangement if the gap between the plates is filled with:
   (a) air
   (b) polystyrene.

If we charge a capacitor of capacitance 1000 pF by connecting it to the terminals of a 3.0V
battery and then the capacitor is removed from the circuit, and is connected it to a small filament
lamp, we will see a brief flash of light. This is the evidence that the capacitor stores energy.
Mobile phones and camera flashes rely on capacitors to store and release the energy they need.
The amount of energy stored in a capacitor depends on the value of the capacitance and the
initial potential difference (p.d.) across it.


Figure 22.12 shows an electron moving towards the negative plate of a capacitor that is being

23.2 Conventional Current - Drift Velocity
People often think that conventional current means the normal, or usual current, but the word
'convention' refers here to an agreement. The scientists who discovered and worked on
electricity agreed to define the direction of current as from the positive terminal of a power
supply to the negative terminal before the electron was discovered in 1897. Unfortunately, this
means that conventional current is in the opposite direction to electron flow. However, not all
currents are due to a flow of electrons. In a solution, or an ionised gas, positive ions flow in the
direction of conventional current.
Imagine a battery connected in series with a switch and a lamp. When we close the switch, we
complete the circuit and the lamp lights up instantaneously, so far as our senses can tell us.
How fast do you think electrons flow through the wires?
The outer electrons in metal atoms are not attracted as strongly to the nucleus as those in atoms
of non-metals. These electrons are free to move between all the atoms (or rather ions, because
they have lost their outermost electrons) in the metal. The metal ions sit like islands in a 'sea'
of free electrons, also called delocalised or conduction electrons.




The free electrons in a metal move around randomly due to their thermal energy with no overall
direction to their movement. However, if a cell or battery is connected across a metal wire, the
free electrons will also be pushed away from its negative terminal and pulled towards its
positive terminal. The average speed at which they move in this direction is called their mean
drift velocity. Mean drift velocity is small compared to the electrons' thermal velocities, but as
the thermal velocities are random, they produce no overall motion of the electrons.


In a metallic conductor, the charge carriers are loosely bound to outer electrons – so-called
‘free’ or ‘delocalised’ electrons. On average, there is approximately one ‘free’ electron per
atom. These ‘free’ electrons move randomly to and fro within the crystal lattice of the metal at
speeds approaching one-thousandth the speed of light and are also mainly responsible for
metals being good conductors of heat. When a potential difference is applied to a circuit, an
electric field is created and exerts a force on the ‘free’ electrons, which causes them to ‘drift’
in the direction of the force.

23.3 Potential difference
To understand how electrons can be made to flow around a circuit and thereby create an
electric current, a comparison with the flow of water in a pipe is often helpful. Such an
analogy is shown in the figure.


In figure a, there is a pressure difference between the water level in the reservoir and that in the
horizontal pipe. When the tap is opened, this pressure difference causes the water to flow
through the pipe and turn the paddle wheel. The gravitational potential energy stored in the
reservoir is converted into kinetic energy of rotation of the paddle wheel.
 In figure b, a chemical reaction in the cell creates an electrical potential difference (symbol
V), which exerts a force on the electrons in the wires. When the switch is closed, this force
causes the electrons to move around the circuit and through the lamp. Here, the chemical
potential energy stored in the cell is converted into vibrational kinetic energy of the atoms in
the filament of the lamp, thereby causing its temperature to rise.
In an electric circuit, electrical energy is converted into other forms of energy – for example in
the circuit of figure b, the lamp converts electrical energy into thermal energy and light.
Conversely, an electric motor converts electrical energy into mechanical energy. In our analogy,
if the paddle wheel in figure a were to be connected to an electric motor, the water could be
pumped up again from the sink to the reservoir.
These energy conversions in electrical circuits form the basis of the definition of potential
difference (often abbreviated to p.d.). The potential difference between two points in a circuit
is the amount of electrical energy converted into other forms of energy (thermal, light,
mechanical, etc) when a unit charge passes from one point to the other. This can be expressed
as:

23.4 Potential Difference and Electromotive Force
Electric current only measures the rate at which the charged particles (usually electrons) flow
around a circuit. It tells us nothing about the electrical energy involved with circuits. The
quantity used to describe the electrical energy in circuits is potential difference (p.d.), symbol
V, measured in volts, V.
A potential difference across an electrical component is measured by putting a voltmeter
across the component, in parallel with it.
 Electrical energy in circuits is defined in terms of the electrical work done by the electric
charge flowing through the circuit. Potential difference (p.d.) is defined as the electrical work
done per unit (coulomb) of charge flowing through components such as bulbs, motors,
resistors, etc. This electrical energy is transferred into heat, light and other more useful forms
of energy by the components.

between these different energy transfers, we define another quantity, electromotive force (emf),
symbol E. Both emf and p.d. are measured in volts, symbol V, using a voltmeter.


Electromotive force (emf) is defined as the electrical work done per unit (coulomb) of charge

23.5 Resistance
When current flows through the material of a circuit, such as the metal of the connecting
wires, the material of the circuit gets in the way of the flow of the charge. On a microscopic
level, as the electrons flow through the metal they collide with the vibrating positive ion cores
of the metal structure. The collisions between the electrons and the positive ion cores transfer
electrical energy from the electrons to the structure of the metal, causing the metal ion cores
to vibrate more, thus heating up the wire.
The opposition of a component to the flow of electric current through it is called resistance,
the symbol is R, and the unit is ohms, Ω.




The model of a metal shown above explains what happens to the resistance of the metal when
it is heated. The resistance increases as the temperature increases. While vibrating the
positively charged ion cores move around more as the temperature increases, thus getting in
the way of electron flow. This opposes the flow of the gas of electrons moving through the
structure. Components with very high resistance let very little current through them, and are
considered to be electrical insulators. Some materials, at very low temperatures, have zero
resistance. These materials are called superconductors.


23.6 Current/Potential Difference Characteristics and Ohm’s Law
Most of the properties of an electrical component can be determined by plotting the current –
potential difference graph of the component. This is called an electrical characteristic.
 Electrical characteristics are graphs that show how the potential difference and current vary
when the component is connected in both forward and reverse bias (when the current passes
one way and then in the other direction). The most straightforward electrical characteristic is
that of a fixed resistor.
You can see that the graph can be drawn with each variable on either axis.




23.6.1 Ohm’s Law
In 1827, the German physicist Georg Ohm performed potential difference–current experiments
on metal wires at constant temperature. Ohm discovered that the current, I, flowing through the
wire was proportional to the potential difference, V, across the wire, provided that the
temperature (and other physical variables) remained constant. If this is shown on an electrical
characteristic graph, then the graph will be linear. The relationship between the current and the
potential difference became known as Ohm’s law, which can be written mathematically by:
                             𝑐𝑢𝑟𝑟𝑒𝑛𝑡 𝐼 ∝ 𝑝𝑜𝑡𝑒𝑛𝑡𝑖𝑎𝑙 𝑑𝑖𝑓𝑓𝑒𝑟𝑒𝑛𝑐𝑒, 𝑉

Ohm’s law applies to some conductors under some circumstances. It is generally a special case
applied to metal wires at constant temperature. But, using the concept of resistance, a
convenient, familiar mathematical equation can be written that uses the relationship between I
and V to define the unit of resistance, the ohm (Ω):
                                                   𝑉
                                              𝑅=
                                                   𝐼
In other words, if a potential difference of 1V produces a current of 1A flowing through a
component, then its resistance must be 1Ω. This defines resistance in ohms. This equation
applies in all cases, and also makes it clear that for a fixed p.d., V, a small measured current, I,
implies that the component has a large resistance, R, and vice versa. Similarly, for a fixed
current, I, we need a large p.d., V, to drive the current through a large resistance, R.
One use of the electrical characteristic graph is that if the current is plotted on the x-axis, for
components following Ohm’s law then the gradient of the line is the same value as the
resistance of the component. As fixed resistors and metal wires at constant temperature have a
fixed resistance, then the electrical characteristic graph will be a straight line.


In this type of graph, high-resistance components have large, steep gradients, and low-
resistance components have small, shallow gradients. Remember though, the electrical
characteristics can be drawn with either variable on either axis. Fixed resistors and metal wires
at constant temperatures obey Ohm’s law across their current range and their electrical
characteristics are linear. Components like this are said to be ohmic conductors, i.e., they obey
Ohm’s law.


23.6.2 Other Electrical Characteristics
 A standard tungsten filament lamp transfers electrical energy into light and heat as the current
flows through it. As the current increases, the frequency of electron collisions with the positive
ion cores of the tungsten lattice increases, transferring more kinetic energy. The positive ion
cores vibrate with greater amplitude and so the resistance increases. A higher current leads to
a higher temperature, which in turn leads to a higher resistance. The electrical characteristic of
a filament lamp is shown in the figure below.




                                   :
                                              𝑉
The electrical characteristic shows the ratio increasing and therefore the resistance increasing.
                                              𝐼
Components like this, whose electrical characteristics are non-linear, are said to be non-ohmic
conductors.
Components such as fixed resistors and filament lamps have the same characteristics
independent of the direction of the current flowing through them. Their V–I graphs produce
the same shapes in forward and reverse bias. Components such as semiconductor diodes do not
behave in this way. Diodes are generally found in electronic circuits where they act as one-way
gates, preventing the current from flowing back through the circuit. They are particularly useful
in mains power supplies where they can be used in circuits to convert alternating current (ac)
into direct current (dc).


Diodes only conduct in forward bias (in the direction of the arrow on the symbol); their circuit
symbol shows this direction using the arrow, and the component itself normally has a different
coloured ring at the forward bias end.




Diodes do not conduct in reverse bias; this means that the resistance of the diode in reverse
bias is infinite. Diodes have very low resistance in forward bias. The electrical characteristics
of diodes are usually drawn in current (y-axis)–potential difference (x-axis) format:




23.6.3 Thermistors
 Thermistors are a type of resistor that change their resistance with temperature. Thermistors
have the following circuit symbol:




Most thermistors are negative temperature coefficient (ntc) components. This means that their
resistance decreases with increasing temperature. The vast majority of ntc thermistors also have
a non-linear response to changing temperature; in other words, a graph of resistance against
temperature is a curve.
 Thermistors are widely used in circuits to sense temperature changes, and then to control
devices; the change in the resistance of the thermistor affects a current, which can be used to
switch devices on or off. They can be found in thermal cut-out circuits to prevent devices from
overheating (such as a hairdryer), central heating circuits, digital thermometers and engine-
management circuits.


23.6.4 Strain Gauge
A strain gauge is made by sealing a length of very fine wire in a small rectangle of thin
plastic, as shown in the figure below.




When the plastic is stretched (the plastic experiences a strain), the wire will also be stretched.
This causes the wire’s length to increase and its cross-sectional area to decrease slightly. Both
these changes cause the resistance of the wire to increase. Strain gauges are usually glued
very securely to the material that is under test.
The resistance R of a wire of length L and of uniform cross-sectional area A is given by the
expression
R = ρL /A,
where ρ is the resistivity of the material of the wire.
Assuming that, when the wire extends by a small amount ∆L, the change in the cross-
sectional area is negligible, the new resistance will be given by,
(R + ∆R) = ρ(L +∆L) /A,
where ∆R is the change in the resistance. Subtracting these two expressions,
∆R = ρ∆L /A
or,
∆R ∝ ∆L.

Thus, the strain which is proportional to the extension ∆L is also proportional to the change in
resistance
∆R. Note that the cross-sectional area A is assumed to be constant.


23.6.5 The Change in Resistance with Light Intensity of a Light-dependent Resistor
(LDR)
A light-dependent resistor (LDR) may be made by sandwiching a film of cadmium sulphide
between two metal electrodes. Typically, in moonlight, its resistance is about 1 MΩ and in
sunlight, 100 Ω. The symbol for an LDR is shown in the figure below.


The resistance of an LDR is constant at constant light intensity.
An LDR is sensitive to changes in light intensity. Note that the change in resistance with
change in light intensity is not linear.


23.5.6 The Temperature Characteristic of a Negative Temperature Coefficient
Thermistor
The resistance of most substances does change slightly with a change in temperature.
However, a thermistor is a device that is manufactured in various shapes and sizes using the
oxides of different metals so that there is a significant change in resistance with temperature.
The symbol for a thermistor is shown in the figure below.




Negative temperature coefficient thermistors have a resistance that becomes less as the
temperature of the thermistor rises. The change in resistance R with temperature θ for a
typical thermistor is illustrated in the figure below.




It can be seen that there is a comparatively largeer change in resistance with temperature but
this change is non-linear.


23.7 Resistivity
How is the intrinsic ‘resistance’ of different materials compared? How do you decide which
material would be best for the internal connections of a mains plug, or for using as an insulator
on a high-voltage line? The resistance of a metal wire, for example, depends on the length and
area of the wire, as well as the material that the wire is made from. Consider figure 13.28,
showing a metal conductor.




The resistance of the conductor, R, increases with increasing length, l (There are more positive
ion cores in the way of the gas of electrons moving through the conductor.). In fact, if the
length, l, doubles, then the resistance, R, doubles. This means that 𝑅 ∝ 𝑙.

The resistance of the conductor decreases with increasing cross-sectional area, A. (There are
more conducting pathways through the conductor for the electrons to move through.) In this
case, if the cross-sectional area, A, doubles, then the resistance, R, halves. This means that 𝑅 ∝

                                                  𝜌×𝑙
                                             𝑅=

where ρ (‘rho’) is called the electrical resistivity of the material. Resistivity is the property that
gives the intrinsic resistance of the material independent of its physical dimensions, such as
length and cross-sectional area. Resistivity has the units of ohm metres, Ωm, and is defined by
the rearranged form of the equation:

where R is the resistance (measured in ohms, Ω), A is the cross-sectional area (measured in
metres squared, m2 ) and l is the length (measured in metres, m).
The resistivity of a material depends on some intrinsic properties of the material. In particular,
it relates directly to the number of free, conducting electrons that can flow through the structure
and the mobility of these electrons to flow through the structure. The arrangement of the atoms
in the conductor and any distribution of impurities affects this mobility, as does the temperature
of the material.


At room temperature (20°C), good insulating materials, such as ABS plastic (the material that
most mains plugs are now made from), have extremely high resistivity (ABS has an electrical
resistivity of  1 × 1015 Ωm at 20°C).
Good metallic conductors have very low resistivity; the resistivity of copper, for example, is
1.68 × 10−8 Ωm at 20°C. Superconductors have zero resistivity below their critical temperature.
We can use a water analogy to help understand resistivity. A hose pipe full of sand is like a high
resistivity conductor, as water trickles through slowly when pressure is applied. However, that
same pressure pushes water quickly through an empty hose pipe, which is like a low resistivity
conductor. Remember though that the ability of the water to pass through the hose pipe also
depends on the length of the hose pipe and its cross-sectional area.
 Resistivity is also dependent on temperature. The resistivity of metals increases with
increasing temperature, and the resistivity of many semiconductors, such as silicon and
germanium, decreases with increasing temperature. The resistivity of a superconducting
material decreases with decreasing temperature above its critical temperature (like a metal),
but its resistivity drops to zero below the critical temperature.

23.10 Potential Dividers
The potential divider is a device that uses two resistances to divide an input potential difference
into smaller values. It can provide a set or varying p.d. output, which becomes the input for a
further circuit, or it can be used in making measurements of p.d. or resistance.

23.10.2 Potential Dividers as Sensors
The use of the potential divider is in sensor circuits. If the variable resistor, R 2 , in the potential
divider circuit shown in the figure is replaced with a component whose resistance varies with
an external physical variable such as temperature or light intensity, then the potential difference
across the fixed resistor, R 1 , will also vary with the external physical variable.


The voltmeter connected across R 1 can then be calibrated in terms of the value of the external
physical variable. The circuit can then be made to act as an electronic thermometer or an
electronic light sensor.
With an electronic thermometer, a thermistor is connected in place of R 2 . Most thermistors are
NTC (negative temperature coefficient) thermistors. This means that as the temperature
increases, their resistance decreases, as shown in figure, which also shows a circuit diagram
showing how the components are connected:




The effect on the potential difference across the fixed resistor R 1 is that as the temperature
increases, so the resistance of the thermistor, R 2 , drops and V 1 rises. Thus, increasing
temperature produces increasing p.d. If the voltmeter is connected across the thermistor, the
opposite will happen: increasing the temperature will produce a decrease in p.d. In most cases,
applications require the p.d. to increase with temperature, so the voltmeter is usually connected
across the fixed resistor.
A similar effect involves the use of a light-dependent resistor (LDR). These are components
that change their resistance with light intensity, which makes them incredibly useful as light
sensors. LDRs are made of semi-conducting materials; as the light shines on the material,
electrons are freed from the structure and can flow through it, reducing the resistance of the
LDR.
In the dark, LDRs can have very high resistance, of the order of megaohms, and yet in the light,
their resistance can drop as low as a few hundred ohms. If an LDR is connected to a potential
divider in place of R 2 in the potential divider circuit then, as the light intensity increases, then
so will the output p.d. V 1 across the fixed resistor.

23.11 Internal Resistance and Electromotive Force
The potential difference across the terminals of a cell (the terminal potential difference)
depends on the size of the current being drawn from the cell. If no current is being drawn (i.e.,
if the cell is on an open circuit), the terminal potential difference has its maximum value -
known as the electromotive force (EMF) of the cell.
The chemicals within a cell offer a resistance to the flow of the current, known as the internal
resistance of the cell. When a cell is connected across an external circuit (a load) some of the
EMF is used to drive current through the load and the rest of the EMF drives the same current
through the internal resistance.
The internal resistance behaves as if it is in series with the cell and the external circuit.
The chemical action inside a battery produces a surplus of electrons at one of its terminals (the
negative), and creates a shortage at the other (the positive). It is then able to maintain a flow of
electrons, i.e., an electric current, in any circuit connected across its terminals for as long as the
chemical action lasts. A work is done by the battery in moving charge around the circuit.
Electromotive force (e.m.f.), symbol E, is defined as the electrical work, W, done by a source
in moving a unit charge around a complete circuit:
                                           𝑤𝑜𝑟𝑘 𝑑𝑜𝑛𝑒 (𝑏𝑦 𝑎 𝑠𝑜𝑢𝑟𝑐𝑒)

Point to remember:
Electromotive force e.m.f. is the electrical work done by a source in moving unit charge around
a complete circuit.
Potential difference p.d. is the work done by a unit charge passing through a component.
In an electric circuit, an electric current transfers energy from an energy store, such as a battery,
to components in the circuit which then transfer energy into the surroundings. In the case of a
lamp, energy is transferred to the surroundings by light and by heating.
Real power supplies, such as batteries and laboratory power packs, always have an internal
resistance, r. As the current flows through the power supply, the internal resistance creates a
potential difference that leads to electrical energy being transferred to thermal energy inside
the power supply. This is one of the reasons why hand-held devices such as tablets warm up
when they are in use for a long period of time.
The internal resistance of most batteries and power supplies is very low: a typical AA battery
has an internal resistance of about 0.2Ω and, as such, can effectively be ignored when
measuring the electrical properties of most circuits.
The internal resistance of a power supply cannot be measured directly as it is ‘inside’ the power
supply. The only way to measure it is to use its electrical characteristics. A circuit that can be
used to do this is shown in the figure below.




Circuit calculations can be used to determine the internal resistance and the electromotive
force.
The electromotive force, E, must be the same as the sum of the potential differences in the
circuit (Conservation of energy). There are two potential differences in this circuit: one is across
the external variable resistor, V, and the other is the p.d. across the internal resistor. This
cannot be measured directly, but the p.d. across this resistor is equal to Ir. This means that:
                                            𝐸 = 𝑉 + 𝐼𝑟

which is the equation of a straight line of the form, y = mx + c, where the gradient is negative.
If an electrical characteristic is drawn using values of V and I from various values of R (the
external load resistance) then the y-intercept of the graph is the electromotive force, E, and the
gradient is negative and equal to –r, the internal resistance.

                                                        𝑅+𝑟
